Teacher Note
Curriculum link: Australian Curriculum: HASS v9, Year 5 
(History)
AC9HS5K03: “the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations 
Australians and those who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an 
Australian colony”. A listed elaboration names “the impact of the Eureka Stockade on the 
development of democracy”, and another poses “What if Peter Lalor had encouraged gold 
miners to pay rather than resist licence fees?”
Skills: AC9HS5S02, “to locate, collect and organise information and data from primary 
and secondary sources in a range of formats”; AC9HS5S04, “to evaluate primary and 
secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives”. Also supports 
AC9HS5S01 (developing questions) and the civics description AC9HS5K07 (citizens 
working together towards a civic goal).
What’s true? Nell’s Diary
This note is for teachers. It is not printed in the student-facing diary, which is written to 
look authentic.
Who is made up? Nell, her father, mother and the baby are invented, as are the trooper 
at the licence hunt, Nell borrowing an onion, everything the Byrnes say and do, her class-
work headings, the place lines at the head of each entry, and Mrs Hayes’s margin notes, 
hint notes, spelling corrections and words to Nell. The Byrnes are Irish, like many families 
near the Eureka lead. Chinese diggers worked the Ballarat goldfield and paid licence fees, 
but no particular Chinese person here is named or invented.
Who is real? Peter Lalor, Captain John Wellesley Thomas, Raffaello Carboni, Anastasia 
Hayes and Timothy Hayes were all real. Their actions come from the case-file sources. 
Lalor’s words on the stump are retold, not quoted; the oath, kneeling and “Amen” come 
from Carboni’s 1855 book. Later notices say she pushed through the soldiers to reach her 
chained husband and told his guards what she thought of them, but her exact words are not 
certain. A later tradition credits Anastasia Hayes with helping to sew the Southern Cross 
flag. That claim is disputed. She is also said to have nursed the wounded.
The school and the sketch Mrs Hayes taught at the Roman Catholic school Dean 
Matthew Downing opened on 1 April 1853 in the slab-and-canvas St Alipius chapel, Ballarat 
East (now St Alipius Parish School, Victoria Street). The image on the diary is Eugene von 
Guérard’s January 1854 sketch Catholic Chapel on the Gravel Pit Line, Ballarat, State 
Library of Victoria, accession H12532 (this work is out of copyright; no copyright 
restrictions apply): https://viewer.slv.vic.gov.au/?entity=IE1446748 The spelling is Alipius.

Sources: https://saballarat.catholic.edu.au/st-alipius-history.html and 
https://eurekapedia.org/Anastasia_Hayes.
What really happened? From the records: the licence hunts; licences burnt on Bakery 
Hill on 29 November; stone-throwing on 30 November; the oath under the flag; the slab 
stockade; the notice about lights; Carboni frying steak and noting the empty stockade on 
Saturday; and the soldiers’ silent march before dawn on 3 December. From her tent, Nell 
could not have known the soldiers’ numbers or their time of march. She only saw what she 
could see, in the dark.
What isn’t certain? Witnesses disagree on the time of the attack. Nobody knows exactly 
how many died: diggers, soldiers, and at least one woman. People still argue about who 
sewed the flag (women of the goldfields, or tent makers or men using tent cloth) and who 
fired first.
What happened next? The stockade was taken in minutes. Lalor was badly wounded 
and hidden by friends. Thirteen men, including Timothy Hayes and Raffaello Carboni, were 
tried for high treason in 1855 and found not guilty. The licence was soon replaced, and 
Lalor was later elected to Victoria’s parliament.
Students may trust the diary as real. Reveal that Nell is invented and ask how they could 
have checked.
An easy-read version in plain hand-print is available online (Easy-read switch) for 
students who find the joined hand hard to read.
What’s true? The case
Peter Lalor, Captain John Wellesley Thomas and Raffaello Carboni were all real. The short 
summaries use their own writing. Words in quotation marks come from Lalor’s 1855 letter, 
Thomas’s report of 3 December 1854, and Carboni’s book of 1855. Nothing on the witness 
page is a reconstruction.

“From a photograph by C. Vandyk.” The 1894 book is out of copyright. Carl Vandyk (1851–1931)

Anastasia Hayes was a real teacher at St Alipius and the wife of digger leader Timothy

more rigorous finding: evidence for, evidence against, and what we still can’t know, with a

Inquiry skills in this case

Asking of every source: who wrote it, when, for whom, and were they there?

Noticing careful words, such as “I believe”, “signal shot” and “volley”.

Noticing Mrs Hayes’s questions in the margin of Nell’s Diary, and asking the 
same of the three witnesses.

Recording disagreement without forcing an answer, and judging how sure a 
finding can be.
Running it in three lessons
Lesson
What happens
1. Read
Read Nell’s Diary together. Notice Mrs Hayes’s margin questions, such as 
“How do you know?” and “What couldn’t you see?” The last entry breaks off 
at the first shot. Teach: licence, stockade, sentry, volley.
2. Ask
Read the short case page. Look at each witness’s picture, the short 
summary, and the source. Answer the same three questions for Lalor, 
Thomas and Carboni: What did they say they saw? Could they really have 
seen it? Why might they say it?
3. Decide
Students write a finding: Who fired first? Rebels, soldiers, or we can’t know 
— and why. Share findings and compare. Close with: how did Eureka affect 
the way the colony was governed?

In front of a banner, Young, New South Wales
Painted 1861 · Still here
The banner is still here.
Someone painted it on a tent flap in 1861. ROLL UP. NO CHINESE. A 
cross, and stars, and those words, big enough to carry at the 
front of a march. And then someone kept it. And then a museum put 
it behind glass, as if it were only an object.
I stood in front of it and tried to imagine two or three thousand 
people walking behind that cloth, toward camps of men who had 
come here to dig. I tried to imagine the petitions that came 
after, written in English and in Chinese, asking to be paid for 
what was taken and smashed. I tried to imagine the courtroom 
where almost everyone walked free.
The banner survived. I’m not sure the people it was 
aimed at were meant to. Who started it, and did anyone 
pay? The file is still open. The cloth is still here.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
This file includes racist violence against Chinese miners, including beatings and the cutting of a 
man’s hair. Teach it with care. The opening notebook is written for this file; what’s true sits in the 
teacher notes. Young is on Wiradjuri Country. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.
CASE 6 · YEAR 9 · THE LAMBING FLAT RIOTS, 1860–61 · READ
The Lambing Flat riots, 1860–61
Who started it, and did anyone pay?
What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.
The Lambing Flat riots were a series of anti-Chinese attacks on the Burrangong goldfield, New 
South Wales, between November 1860 and July 1861. Lambing Flat was one part of the field. 
The main settlement later became the town of Young. The Riot Act was read on 27 January and 
on 14 July 1861.
The first anti-Chinese riot on this field is dated 13 November 1860. Further attacks followed, 
including 8–9 December 1860, 27 January 1861, and 19 February 1861. On 8–9 December, 
reports of two Chinese deaths were investigated by Superintendent Henry Zouch of the Mounted 
Police, who found that no deaths had occurred and that the reports had come from European 
miners.
The worst attack was on 30 June 1861. A crowd of European, American and Australasian-born 
miners, commonly put at 2,000 to 3,000, marched with a band and the “Roll Up – No Chinese” 
banner from Allandale (Tipperary Gully) to camps at Sawpit Gully and then Back Creek. 
Numbers of Chinese people at those camps are not agreed in the sources: one careful local 
account gives about 200–600 at Sawpit Gully and 400–1,000 at Back Creek; other accounts 
give different figures. Chinese petitioners later said they were beaten, that property was 
destroyed, and that one of them, Tom Me, had his hair cut off. One later synthesis says about 
200 Chinese people were wounded, and that no one was killed on 30 June. This file records 
those claims, and does not invent a death toll the record has not settled.
The banner, painted on a tent flap, is now held at the Young Historical Museum. It shows a

pages.text:
Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 83
saltire and stars, with the words “Roll Up” and “No Chinese.”
Police arrested men identified as leaders. On the night of 14 July 1861 a crowd attacked the 
police camp; the police broke it up with gunfire and a mounted charge. One rioter, William 
Lupton, was killed. Troops, sailors and police reinforcements later arrived from Sydney and 
remained for a time. Premier Charles Cowper had already visited Burrangong in early March 
1861, between the earlier riots and the June attack.
Most men tried for the riots were acquitted. Two were convicted: Claremont Owen, a 
watchmaker, sentenced to two years’ hard labour in Darlinghurst Gaol for his part in the 14 July 
riot; and William Spicer, a miner, sentenced to two years’ imprisonment for his part in the 30 
June riot. Spicer was released on the Queen’s Birthday in 1862 after a petition of 2,989 
signatures from the Lachlan goldfield. Some later retellings say only Spicer was convicted. This 
file follows the court record that both Owen and Spicer were sentenced.
Chinese miners and storekeepers petitioned the New South Wales government for 
compensation, in English and in Chinese. William Campbell, as a commissioner, examined 
claims. For losses on 30 June 1861 he reported 1,568 claimants asking a total of £40,623, and 
recommended that £4,240 be paid to 706 people. In September 1863 lists of approved claims 
were published in the NSW Government Gazette. In March 1864, 94 Chinese signatories at 
Tuena petitioned that their approved claims had still not been paid, almost three years after the 
riot. Whether the full amount recommended was ever paid remains an open question in the 
sources.
Later in 1861 the New South Wales Parliament passed the Chinese Immigrants Regulation and 
Restriction Act 1861 (often called the Chinese Immigration Restriction Act), which imposed a 
£10 tax on Chinese immigrants arriving by ship. The Gold Fields Act 1861 also allowed the 
restriction of “aliens” on the fields. Those laws sit in the same year as the riots. This file does not 
pretend the Parliament had only one reason for passing them.

What they said
Their petition stated that diggers and “other evil disposed persons” 
assembled “on foot and on horseback, to the number, at various times 
during the said day, of from eight hundred to three thousand, as your 
Petitioners believe,” armed “with bludgeons, fire-arms, and other weapons, 
and carrying banners or flags inscribed with the words “Roll up”, “No 
Chinese.”” They said the crowd “attacked your Petitioners and the rest of 
the Chinese,” beat them, and, “subjecting your Petitioner, Tom Me, to the 
indignity of cutting off his hair, drove your Petitioners and the rest of the 
Chinese, from the said diggings.”
Could they have seen it?
They were there. They could describe what was done to them, and what was 
taken. A petition for money is still a sworn kind of public claim, written to a 
government, in a legal voice that borrowed the language of the Riot Act. 
They were not in the March meeting with the Premier, and they were not 
on the bench in the later trials. Their estimate of the crowd, “from eight 
hundred to three thousand,” already tells you they could not count it 
exactly.
Why might they say it?
To have the damage recognised, and to be paid. A petition can be exact 
about the cutting of Tom Me’s hair, and still be argued over when it comes 
to gold, tents and stores. Students can hold both things: this is one of the 
few places the record lets Chinese miners speak, and it is also a claim for 
compensation.
Source. Petition of Tom Me, What Young and Que You, and others, for compensation for 
damages incurred on 30 June 1861, as quoted from the surviving petitions in the Museums of 
History NSW State Archives, and as published in later documentary work (including the 
Young Historical Museum’s account of the riots). A related earlier petition, of Hu Foo and 
Kylong and others, describes the attack of 19 February in the language of the Riot Act. 
Wording as quoted from those documentary sources. No period portrait of the named 
petitioners has been located. The image is a silhouette, not a likeness.

Charles Cowper
Premier of New South Wales · Visited Burrangong, March 1861 · Died 1875
The head of the government that sent officials to the field, later saw men 
tried, and, in the same year as the worst riot, passed a law to restrict 
Chinese immigration.
What they said
Cowper went to Burrangong in early March 1861, after the summer riots 
and months before 30 June. The Miners’ Protective League had been 
formed in late January. This file does not invent what he said to the miners 
on that visit. What is not in doubt is the later record of his government: 
most rioters tried were acquitted; two were gaoled; and later in 1861 
Parliament passed an Act imposing a £10 tax on Chinese immigrants 
arriving by ship, and a Gold Fields Act that allowed the restriction of 
“aliens.” In 1858 an earlier restriction bill had failed.
Could they have seen it?
He could see the field in March, and he could see Parliament later in the 
year. He could not, from March, have seen the march of 30 June, or the 
attack on the police camp on 14 July. A Premier’s visit is not the same thing 
as standing in the Chinese camp when the banner arrived. He also cannot 
be made to stand in for the petitioners who were still waiting for payment 
in 1864.
Why might they say it?
To keep a goldfield from slipping out of the government’s hands, and to 
answer a political problem about Chinese immigration that had already 
divided his own side. Students can ask whether passing a restriction Act 
after a riot is a way of paying the rioters, or of preventing more violence, or 
both — and whether the people who were beaten were in the room when 
that was decided.
Source. Contemporary newspaper reports of Cowper’s visit, arriving on Saturday 2 March 
1861, and of the later parliamentary passage of the Chinese Immigrants Regulation and 
Restriction Act 1861. This card does not invent a speech for him at Burrangong, and does not 
put quotation marks around words this file has not checked word for word. The portrait is a 
nineteenth-century image, Wikimedia Commons (File:Charlescowper.jpg), public domain. 
No likeness has been invented.

William Campbell
Commissioner examining compensation claims · Report, “Aggressions on 
Chinese,” 29 August 1862
The official who sat between the petitions and the money, and who decided 
that some claims were genuine and some were not.
What they said
For earlier riots, in January and February 1861, Campbell examined 30 
Chinese claimants seeking £6,339 and declared the destruction “very 
trifling, and that the claims herein before referred to are altogether 
fraudulent.” For 30 June 1861 he examined 1,568 claims totalling £40,623, 
recognised 706 as genuine, and recommended £4,240, after deductions. 
Approved names were later gazetted. In 1864, 94 Chinese signatories at 
Tuena said they had been approved and had still not been paid.
Could they have seen it?
He could see the paperwork, and he could examine claimants. He was not 
an eyewitness to the march. A commissioner who calls one set of claims 
“altogether fraudulent” and then allows another set at about a tenth of what 
was asked is making a judgment, not taking a photograph. He also cannot, 
from 1862, tell you whether the gazetted sums were actually paid in 1863 or 
1864.
Why might they say it?
To settle a government problem: how much, if anything, to pay. A report 
that cuts a claim heavily can be careful, or it can be hostile, or both. 
Students can set his “fraudulent” finding beside the 1864 petition from 
people whose claims he had already approved.
Source. William Campbell, “Aggressions on Chinese, Compensation Claimed for Losses 
Sustained During Riots at Burrangong Gold Fields,” 29 August 1862, Votes and Proceedings 
of the Legislative Assembly of New South Wales, 1862, IV, pp. 9–27; and “Claims of Chinese 
to Compensation for Losses during Burrangong Riots,” NSW Government Gazette, 18 
September 1863, pp. 2029–30. The 28 March 1864 Tuena petition of 94 signatories, stating 
that approved claims were still unpaid, is documented in later archival work on the Lands 
and Public Works files. No period portrait of this William Campbell is used here. The image 
is a silhouette, not a likeness.

My finding
The three witness cards are the Chinese petitioners, Charles Cowper, and William Campbell. Further questions — 
including the troops, the 14 July attack, and whether the 1861 Act was a kind of payment — are in Super Sleuths.
You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is 
not an 1861 diary, and the banner emblem is a reconstruction of the wording and layout, not a 
photograph of the museum object. Say what you think the records can prove about who started 
the riots, and whether anyone paid — in gaol, or in compensation, or in a new law. “We can’t 
know” is an honest finding when the sources disagree, or when payment that was recommended 
cannot be shown to have been made. Do not invent what the petitions and the reports do not 
say.
Who started it, and did anyone pay?
Circle one: A few ringleaders started it, and two of them paid in gaol · A much larger crowd started 
it, and almost no one paid · The government paid some compensation, but we can’t tell if the money 
arrived · The 1861 Act was a different kind of payment, and it was made to the rioters, not to the 
people beaten · We can’t know, from this file, who first called “roll up,” or whether every approved 
claim was paid · Another finding, written below
MY FINDING
My finding. ________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________
The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
______________________________________________________________
What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
______________________________________________________________
Why it still matters
The banner was kept. The petitions almost were not. Lambing Flat is still used, sometimes, as a 
colourful goldfields story, and sometimes as a starting-point for later White Australia laws. The 
file is open because a riot can have many hands, because a court can acquit almost everyone, 
and because a sum written in a report is not the same thing as money in a claimant’s hand. Who 
a nation decides to protect, after a crowd has already done the damage, is not only a question 
about 1861.

Super Sleuths
Go further only if you want to. Amber marks what is still disputed, or what later writers added. Young 
is on Wiradjuri Country. This file does not tell a Wiradjuri history of the goldfield, and does not invent 
one.
Open these investigations in the app: robmac10.github.io/lambing-flat-case/#sleuth
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
1. The notebook is written for this file
The typographic page is a constructed student voice, standing in front of the Roll Up banner at the 
Young Historical Museum. The narrator is not a historical person. The opener does not invent 1861 
dialogue. “Two or three thousand” is a range, not a head-count, and the agreed file says the numbers 
are disputed.
Question. What is the difference between imagining yourself in front of a surviving object, and 
inventing a speech for the people who marched behind it?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
2. Who started it?
There was not one riot and not one starter. A Vigilance Committee and, later, a Miners’ Protective 
League formed on the field. “Roll up” was a call to gather. Notices to quit were posted. A brass band 
led some of the marches. The 30 June crowd is often described as taking over a miners’ meeting. The 
record does not give you a single name at the front of the first November attack and still let you call 
the question settled.
Question. If a file cannot name one starter, what finding is still honest — and what finding would be a 
guess?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
3. Numbers that do not agree
Crowd estimates for 30 June run from the petitioners’ “eight hundred to three thousand” to the 
common later figure of 2,000–3,000. Numbers in the Chinese camps vary widely between accounts. 
Reports of two Chinese deaths in December 1860 were investigated and not upheld. A later synthesis 
says about 200 people were wounded on 30 June, and that no one was killed that day. William 
Lupton was killed on 14 July, in the attack on the police camp.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. One convicted man, or two?
Some later retellings say only William Spicer was convicted. The court record used here is that 
Claremont Owen and William Spicer were both sentenced to two years, and that Spicer was released 
early after a large petition. Two unconvicted rioters are sometimes later said to have been elected to 
parliament. That last claim is not treated as agreed in this file without a named, checked source.
Question. What happens to the question “did anyone pay?” if a later story quietly drops one of the 
two convicted men?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Recommended is not the same as paid
Campbell recommended £4,240 to 706 people out of £40,623 claimed by 1,568. Lists were gazetted 
in 1863. In March 1864, 94 signatories at Tuena said approved claims were still unpaid. Some later 
writers have doubted whether compensation was paid at all. This file leaves that question open. The 
earlier January–February claims he called “altogether fraudulent” are part of the same official story, 
and should not be hidden.
Question. If you were writing a finding about payment, what would you need to see before you said 
“yes, they were paid”?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. The 1861 Act, and a longer shadow
The Chinese Immigrants Regulation and Restriction Act 1861 imposed a £10 arrival tax. It is often 
treated as a direct result of Lambing Flat. The colony had already argued over a restriction bill in 
1858. The riots, a petition from thousands of European miners, and the parliamentary debate all sit 
close together. Later writers have also drawn a line from this banner to the Immigration Restriction 
Act 1901. That line is an argument, not a fact the 1861 parchment itself can prove.
Question. Is a new tax on Chinese arrivals a kind of payment to the rioters? What evidence would you 
use, and what would you still not know?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. The banner in the museum
The 1861 banner survives at Young. The QR emblem in this file is a reconstruction of its wording and 
layout, not a photograph of the object. Keeping a banner can be memory, warning, or pride, 
depending on who is doing the keeping. Karen Schamberger and others have written about how this 
“difficult history” is shown in a local museum.
Question. If a museum keeps the banner, what else has to be in the same room — the petitions, the 
acquittals, the unpaid claims — for the display to be a history, and not only a relic?
8. Sure, maybe, or a guess?
Sure: there were repeated anti-Chinese attacks at Burrangong in 1860–61; a banner with “Roll Up” 
and “No Chinese” was carried; most accused men were acquitted; Owen and Spicer were convicted; 
Chinese petitioners described beatings and the cutting of Tom Me’s hair; Campbell recommended 
£4,240; an 1861 Act put a £10 tax on Chinese arrivals by ship. Maybe: whether every gazetted pound 
was paid; exact camp numbers on 30 June. A guess: a single starter’s name, or the private thoughts 
of a man walking behind the banner. The opener is not a source for 1861.
Question. Write a finding of no more than five sentences, and mark each sentence sure, maybe, or a 
guess.

CASE 6 · YEAR 9 · THE LAMBING FLAT RIOTS, 1860–61 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page. The user’s name is kept off the student pages and off 
the app.
What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed student notebook, written for this file, in the voice of a 
later visitor standing in front of the Roll Up banner at the Young Historical Museum. It is not 
an 1861 diary. It does not invent dialogue, and it does not treat “two or three thousand” as a 
precise count. The QR emblem is a reconstruction of the wording and layout of the 1861 banner, 
not a photograph of the museum object (even though a photograph of the banner circulates on 
Wikimedia Commons as public domain).
Curriculum
The brief asked for an accurate AC9HS9 code, and suggested Year 9. There is no AC9HS9. Year 
9 History uses AC9HH9 codes. The lead code is AC9HH9K04: significant events, ideas, people, 
groups and movements in the development of Australian society, in the “Making and 
transforming the Australian nation (1750–1914)” depth study. AC9HH9K02 and AC9HH9K07 
are related, and may be mentioned to teachers; they are not claimed as lead codes on the 
student pages.
Source conflicts, flagged
Crowd and camp numbers for 30 June disagree. December 1860 death reports were 
investigated and not upheld; later writing still has to be watched for a creeping death toll. Some 
popular accounts say only Spicer was convicted; this file follows Owen and Spicer. Campbell 
recommended payment; a Gazette published names; an 1864 petition says approved money had 
not arrived; some later writers doubt payment was made. The official short title of the 1861 Act 
is given here as the Chinese Immigrants Regulation and Restriction Act 1861, also commonly 
called the Chinese Immigration Restriction Act; if a teacher has the enacted title in a slightly 
different form, this note should be corrected. Claims that unconvicted rioters later entered 
parliament are not treated as agreed without a checked source.
Race, violence, and care
This is a file about racist violence. The cutting of Tom Me’s hair was an assault and a 
humiliation, and is named in his petition. Beatings are named, not described for shock. Chinese 
names appear as they do in the English petitions, which are themselves transliterations; where 
Chinese characters survive on the archival petitions, teachers may wish to show that page. 
Living descendants deserve care. The banner’s language is quoted because it is the object, not 
because it should be treated as ordinary classroom talk.

Friday, 28 June 1861.
Cooper Creek
Clear, cold night; slight breeze from the E.; day beautifully warm 
and pleasant. Mr Burke suffers greatly from the cold, and is 
getting extremely weak. He and King start tomorrow up the creek … 
it is the only chance we have of being saved from starvation.
I am weaker than ever, although I have a good appetite and relish 
the nardoo much; but it seems to give us no nutriment …
Nothing now but the greatest good luck can save any of us; and as 
for myself I may live four or five days if the weather continues 
warm. My pulse is at forty-eight, and very weak, and my legs and 
arms are nearly skin and bone. I can only look out, like Mr 
Micawber, “for something to turn up.” Starvation on nardoo is by no 
means very unpleasant, but for the weakness one feels, and the 
utter inability to move oneself; for as far as appetite is concerned, 
it gives me the greatest satisfaction.
W. J. Wills

What was the real cause of death?
Burke and Wills at Cooper Creek, 1861
Draft, pending consultation with Yandruwandha Yawarrawarrka and related communities, and with 
AIATSIS guidance.
Read the notebook page through to the last line. Then read what the 1861 file can agree on. After 
that, three people will be asked the same three questions.
CASE FILE: BURKE AND WILLS / 1861
Date of incident April–September 1861 (depot: 21 April; last notebook: late June; King 
found: 15 September)
Location Cooper Creek, in Yandruwandha country
Status Unresolved contradictions · Draft, pending consultation
Key claims still disputed
– What was the real cause of death — hunger, the missed depot, the nardoo itself, the cold, 
or more than one of these?
– Whose record should we trust — Wills’s notebook, King’s later narrative, or Howitt’s 
diary of the rescue?
– What does the 1861 file leave unasked about the Yandruwandha people who kept King 
alive?
WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1861 FILE, AND AFTER
In 1860 a party left Melbourne to cross the continent from south to north. Robert O’Hara Burke led it. 
William John Wills was the surveyor. John King and Charles Gray went north with them from the Cooper 
Creek depot. (Some newspapers of the time wrote Grey. The expedition records usually write Gray.)
The four reached the Gulf country and turned back. Gray died on 17 April 1861, on the return, before they 
reached the depot.
On the evening of 21 April 1861, Burke, Wills and King reached the depot with two camels and almost no 
food. The depot party, led by William Brahe, had left that same morning. Stores had been buried, and a 
tree was marked so a returning party would know to dig. The exact wording cut into the tree is uncertain: 
sources disagree.
They tried to make south towards Mount Hopeless, then came back to the creek. Both remaining camels 
died. They tried to live on nardoo — a fern seed used as food by the Yandruwandha people of the Cooper — 
and on fish and gifts they were given.
On 30 May 1861 Wills went back to the depot and left a note in the buried cache. The depot was still 
empty. Unseen by him, Brahe and Wright had visited the cache earlier in May, thought it untouched, and 
left again. The wording of that 30 May note is in Super Sleuths. It is not the same document as the last 
notebook page at the front of this case.
Wills’s last notebook entry is from late June 1861. He wrote that nardoo seemed to give them “no

nutriment,” that his pulse was at forty-eight, and that he could only look out, like Mr Micawber, “for 
something to turn up.” Burke and King then went up the creek for help, leaving food and water with him.
Burke died a short time later. King later found Wills already dead. The exact days are not known. King was 
found alive on 15 September 1861 by Alfred Howitt’s relief party, after living with Yandruwandha people 
along the creek.
In 1994, J. W. Earl and B. V. McCleary argued in the journal Nature that nardoo can destroy the vitamin 
thiamine, and that Burke and Wills may have died of beriberi as well as of hunger and cold. That is a later 
scientific reading, not something the 1861 file could know. It is still debated.
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.

Three witnesses
The same three questions for each: What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · 
Why might they say it? Each has a period photograph, used because the licence is clear. No likeness 
of a real person has been invented.
A NOTE ON THE LANGUAGE OF THE RECORDS
Some 1861 records use the language of the time, including words this file does not use as its own. 
Short attributed extracts are in Super Sleuths, with a content note. They are not the language of this 
case file.

Photograph, about 1860, by 
Thomas Adams Hill. Public 
domain.
William John Wills
Surveyor of the expedition · 1834–1861
His Cooper Creek field notebook, recovered after his death.
Source. National Library of Australia, MS 30/7, journal of the trip from Cooper Creek towards Adelaide, 23 
April to late June 1861. A widely printed wording of the last entry is used on the opening page and on this 
card; date and wording variants are set out in the Teacher Note.
What they said. In the last entry he wrote that he still had an appetite and relished the 
nardoo, “but it seems to give us no nutriment.” He thought he might live four or five days if 
the weather stayed warm. “My pulse is at forty-eight, and very weak, and my legs and arms 
are nearly skin and bone. I can only look out, like Mr Micawber, ‘for something to turn up.’” 
A few days earlier he had written that he could not understand the nardoo at all: it would 
not agree with him in any form.
Could they really have seen it? He was there, writing in his own notebook as his strength 
failed. He could record what he felt and what he ate. He could not see what would happen after 
Burke and King left, and he could not test, as later scientists have tried to, why the nardoo 
seemed to give no nutriment.
Why might they say it? To leave a record, and a last message, in case someone came. A man 
writing as he grows weaker is close to the event, but he is not a doctor, and he is writing his own 
ending.
What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________
Photograph, about 1861. 
Public domain.
John King
The only member of the northern party to survive · 1838–1872
A narrative taken down for Howitt at Cooper Creek in September 1861, later given to the 
Commission of Enquiry.
Source. “Narrative of John King,” written up by Alfred Howitt from notes in his field-book, State Library of 
Victoria, MS 13071. King told it weeks after the deaths, when he was still very weak.
What they said. He said the three of them reached the depot on the evening of 21 April 
and found that the party had gone the same day. They dug up the buried stores. Later, 
when they were too weak to keep collecting food, Wills asked to be left with a supply, and 
they buried the rest of his field-books by his hut. Burke asked him again whether he still 
wished it. King said that Burke, on the last evening, asked him to stay until he was dead, 
and to leave him as he lay. King found him gone the next morning. Days later he found 
Wills already dead, and later still he lived on what Yandruwandha people gave him until the 
relief party came.
Could they really have seen it? He was the only one of the three still alive. He had been at 
the depot on 21 April, on the last walk with Burke, and at Wills’s hut when he returned. No one 
else from the party could check his account. He told it after weeks of hunger, and Howitt wrote it 
down.
Why might they say it? Howitt needed a report to take back to Melbourne, and King was the 
only survivor who had been there. Memory, weakness, and the wish to explain what had 
happened can all shape a story told after the event.

Alfred Howitt
Leader of the Victorian relief party · 1830–1908
His own diary of the day his party found King.
Source. A. W. Howitt, diary of the Victorian Contingent Expedition, State Library of Victoria, MS 13071, 
entry for Sunday, 15 September 1861. Published in the Melbourne press after the party returned.
What they said. On 15 September 1861 Howitt wrote that he was still following tracks 
when two of his party came with the news that King, the only survivor of Burke’s party, had 
been found. He went across to the huts and found King sitting in a hut that the people of 
the creek had made for him. King, he wrote, “presented a melancholy appearance — wasted 
to a shadow,” and seemed exceedingly weak, so that Howitt sometimes found it hard to 
follow what he said. The people of the camp were gathered round, looking, Howitt wrote, 
gratified and delighted. He decided to stay about ten days to let King recover before starting 
back.
Could they really have seen it? He was there the day King was found, and he wrote it in his 
diary that same day. He did not see Burke or Wills die, and he was not the first of his party to 
reach King: others found him, and Howitt came across a little later. What he records of the 
deaths is what King told him.
Why might they say it? He had been sent to find the missing party and to report. A diary 
written the same day is close to the rescue. It is still one man’s view, and it is not a 
Yandruwandha account of the same day.
What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________

What was the real cause of death?

MY FINDING
My reason:
Why it still matters
Burke and Wills are still told as a heroic crossing, or as a bungled meeting at a tree. The file 
is open because the records do not settle what killed them, and because the people who 
kept King alive have not always been asked. Draft, pending consultation with

Optional, and a little harder. These questions stay in the file because the record is not settled. 
You can also open them in the interactive book.
Open Super Sleuths in the app: robmac10.github.io/burke-wills-case/#sleuth
THE LANGUAGE OF THE 1861 RECORDS
Content note. The extracts below keep a few words from 1861 records that this case file does not use 
as its own, including “blacks” and “natives.” They are short, attributed quotations. They are not the 
language of this book.
1 · TWO DIFFERENT DOCUMENTS
Wills wrote the 30 May 1861 cache note at the depot and buried it in the camel-box cache (State 
Library of Victoria, MS 13071, SAFE 1, “Last notes”). A careful transcription of the two pages reads, in 
part:
“Depot Camp, May 30th. We have been unable to leave the creek. Both camels are dead, and our 
provisions are exhausted. Mr Burke and King are down the lower part of the creek. I am about to 
return to them, when we shall probably come up this way. We are trying to live the best way we can, 
like the blacks, but find it hard work. Our clothes are going to pieces fast. Send provisions and clothes 
as soon as possible. W J Wills. The Depot party having left, contrary to instructions, has put us in this 
fix. I have deposited some of my journals here for fear of accidents. W J W.”
That note does not contain “my pulse is at forty-eight,” “skin and bone,” or “it seems to give us no 
nutriment.” Those lines are from the later field notebook (NLA MS 30/7), used at the front of this 
case. Why does it matter if a later writer mixes the two documents into one page?
2 · THE TREE, AND WHY NO ONE WAS WAITING
King, in his 1861 narrative, remembered a tree marked “DIG, Apr 21.” Popular tellings often give 
“DIG 3 FT NW.” The Dig Tree site and later writers also record date blazes (including December 1860 
and 21 April 1861), a camp mark often read as B LXV (Burke, Camp 65), and a later mark by Howitt, 
AH DIG. A National Trust plaque notes that the Burke party recalled a depth of three feet, while 
some early settlers remembered forty feet. John White and later research list still more published 
variants. Brahe told the Commission he marked a tree with the date 21 April, and also a December 
date.
Why was no one waiting at the Dig Tree? That was this case’s first outlined question. Brahe had 
already waited about four months. One of his party, Patton, was badly hurt. On 21 April he left for the 
Darling — the same morning the three men came in. In early May, Brahe and Wright returned, 
thought the cache untouched, and left again, before Wills came back on 30 May. What can we 
actually agree about the tree, and what is still in dispute?

3 · THE 1994 NATURE PAPER
J. W. Earl and B. V. McCleary, “Mystery of the poisoned expedition,” Nature 368 (21 April 1994): 
683–684, argued that nardoo (Marsilea drummondii) contains thiaminase, an enzyme that destroys 
vitamin B1 (thiamine), and that Burke and Wills may have died of beriberi as well as of hunger. An 
earlier paper, McCleary and Chick, Phytochemistry 16 (1977), had identified thiaminase in nardoo. 
Yandruwandha preparation of the seed is part of the argument: the explorers may not have prepared 
it in the same way. John Hayman wrote a follow-up letter in Nature 370 (1994). The 1994 paper is a 
hypothesis, not an autopsy, and it is still debated.
Wills himself had already written that the nardoo seemed to give “no nutriment,” and that he could 
not understand it. How far can a later scientific paper settle a question the 1861 file left open?
4 · WHAT THE 1861 FILE DID NOT ASK
This draft does not put “the Yandruwandha people” on a witness card. A group is not one witness, 
and this file is pending consultation with Yandruwandha Yawarrawarrka and related communities, 
and with AIATSIS guidance.
Published starting points, for reading with community guidance, include: Benny Kerwin’s 
Yandruwandha narrative, transcribed by Gavan Breen, in Luise Hercus and Peter Sutton (eds), This 
Is What Happened: Historical Narratives by Aborigines (Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies, 
1986); the listing for the Burke, Wills, King and Yandruwandha National Heritage Place (DCCEEW); 
Wills’s diary for 3 June 1861, in which a man he names Pitchery feeds him fish and nardoo; and 
King’s narrative of being fed, and of the people who wept over Burke’s remains and covered them 
with bushes.
What is not asked if we only use the explorers’ notebooks? Whose skill kept King alive?
5 · BURKE’S LAST REQUEST, IN KING’S WORDS
In the narrative Howitt took down, King said that Burke, on the last evening, spoke these words: “I 
hope you will remain with me here till I am quite dead — it is a comfort to know that some one is by; 
but, when I am dying, it is my wish that you should place the pistol in my right hand, and that you 
leave me unburied as I lie.” King said that the following morning, about eight o’clock, Burke died. 
The student card tells the request more quietly, because this is a Year 5 file. Why might Burke have 
asked for that? What can we know, and what can we not?

CASE 7 · YEAR 5 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
Draft, pending consultation with Yandruwandha Yawarrawarrka and related communities, 
and with AIATSIS guidance.
The opening page
The opening page is not constructed, and it must not be labelled “constructed” or “not original” on 
the student page. It is an abridged typographic presentation of William John Wills’s last Cooper 
Creek field-notebook entry (NLA MS 30/7). Ellipses mark two cuts: the clause “to look for the 
blacks,” and a short middle passage about birds and fish, so the page can hold the lines that carry 
the case — “no nutriment,” the pulse at forty-eight, “nearly skin and bone,” and the Mr Micawber 
sentence — without a graphic account of dying and without mixing in the 30 May cache note. The 
closing remarks on fat and sugar were also set aside, so the page ends on the Micawber / nardoo 
lines. A full transcription belongs in class only if you have time and a content note ready.
Date of that last entry: this file prints Friday, 28 June 1861, because 28 June 1861 was a Friday. 
Some published versions print Friday 26 June (a Wednesday; the NLA catalogue also dates the 
notebook 23 April–26 June), or 27 June. Burke and Wills Web flags “Friday, 26 June 1861. [sic: 28 
June?].” A provenance note on that site says Burke and King buried the field-book on 28 June. Do 
not treat a single heading as settled. Wording also varies. A transcription associated with the NLA 
item (and with W. H. Archer’s 1861 copy) has “My pulse are at forty-eight” and “farinacious.” Widely 
printed 1863 / later texts have “My pulse is at forty-eight” and “farinaceous.” This file follows the 
widely printed wording on the student page and flags the variants here.
What the draft mixed, and what was corrected
The supplied draft presented a “note left at the Dig Tree, 30 May 1861,” and labelled it constructed, 
but it mixed the 30 May cache note with later diary lines (“pulse 48,” “skin and bone,” and the 
nardoo / “no nutriment” sentence). Those later lines belong to the last notebook entry, not to SLV 
MS 13071 SAFE 1. The nutriment wording is genuine, but it is diary, not cache-note. Favenc and 
some older printings of the 30 May note also differ in small ways from the two-page SAFE 1 
transcription (for example “down on the lower part” / “going fast to pieces”). This file follows the 
SAFE 1 transcription as given on burkeandwills.net.au, and puts the note in Super Sleuths, not on 
the opening page.
Case number, year level, and curriculum
The draft header was CASE 38 · YEAR 10, with AC9HH10K10 and AC9HH10K11. Those Year 10 
codes are rights-and-freedoms content; in earlier book lists they belonged with the Wave Hill walk-
off, 1966, which is not in this sample. This written file is Case 7, Year 5, AC9HS5K03. That v9 Year 5 
HASS code concerns the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations Australians 
and those who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an Australian colony. The First 
Nations consultation tag is added. The file does not silently take a Year 10 number or those Year 10 
codes.

Dates, names, and other corrections
Return to the depot: evening of 21 April 1861 (King: about half-past seven). Brahe left that morning. 
Charles Gray (not Grey in the usual expedition spelling; some newspapers used Grey) died on 17 
April 1861, before the depot. Wills’s cache note: 30 May 1861. Burke’s and Wills’s deaths: late June 
or very early July 1861; the exact days are not known. King was found on 15 September 1861 
(Howitt’s diary; others in the party reached King first that day, then Howitt). Howitt recovered field-
books from the cache later in September (his diary, 28 September).
King’s testimony about Burke’s pistol request is genuine, in the narrative Howitt took down (SLV 
MS 13071). The exact wording is in Super Sleuths, not in full on the Year 5 witness card. Earl and 
McCleary 1994 is correctly cited as Nature 368, 683–684 (21 April 1994), “Mystery of the poisoned 
expedition.” Treat it as a cited hypothesis, not as the verdict.
Portraits, care, and consultation
The three witness images are period photographs, used because the licence is clear, not invented 
likenesses. Wills: Thomas Adams Hill, about 1860, State Library of New South Wales / Wikimedia 
Commons, public domain. King: photograph, about 1861, SLNSW DL PXX 3 3a / Wikimedia 
Commons, public domain. Howitt: photograph, about 1861, SLNSW DL PXX 3 / Wikimedia 
Commons, public domain. A licence-clear c. 1860 photograph of Burke, also by Thomas Adams Hill 
(National Portrait Gallery of Australia / Wikimedia Commons, public domain), exists but is not used 
as a witness card, because Burke is not one of the three witnesses. Student pages avoid graphic 
detail of the deaths. Living people are not dated on the student pages; no living person is named as a 
witness here.
Yandruwandha perspectives stay in Super Sleuths and in this note until consultation. Published 
sources only are cited (Kerwin / Breen in Hercus and Sutton 1986; the National Heritage Place; 
Wills on Pitchery; King on being fed and on the covering of Burke’s remains). Do not invent a named 
Yandruwandha voice for a third card.

A goldfields track, Western Australia
The 1890s
The dust is the colour of the late sun. A string of camels comes in along the track, 
unhurried, each one loaded. The men walk at their shoulders the way they have 
walked for days.
Someone has been waiting for the water, the flour, the mail. Someone is glad to see 
them.
Someone else is already talking about getting them off the field.
The men who can take a load where horses fail have opened tracks through this 
country. The question in this file is whether the country opened to them.

guidance. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.
CASE 8 · YEAR 5–6 · THE ‘AFGHAN’ CAMELEERS · READ
The ‘Afghan’ cameleers
Were they welcomed, or pushed out?
What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.
From the 1860s, cameleers worked camel transport in the Australian inland. Settlers often 
called them “Afghans.” Many came from Afghanistan, Baluchistan, the Punjab and neighbouring 
regions. The label was a settler word, not a precise map of where every man was born.
In 1862 Sir Thomas Elder imported camels from India into South Australia. In a lecture written 
in 1879 he said he had “partly the furtherance of this object in view” — the exploration of the 
interior — when he imported them, and that the camels had “increased in number from 110 to 
500 or 600.” Cameleers working with those animals carted materials for inland work, including 
the Overland Telegraph Line, built in 1870–72.
Faiz Mahomet managed Elder Smith & Co.’s camel station at Hergott Springs, later called 
Marree. Sources disagree on when he first arrived in Australia: about 1870, in the Australian 
Dictionary of Biography; 31 December 1865, in some later accounts. With his younger brother 
Tagh he moved to the Western Australian goldfields in 1892 and set up camel stations and stores 
in Coolgardie, Geraldton, Cue, Day Dawn and Mullewa.
In 1895 Faiz petitioned for the protection of his countrymen’s lives and property against threats 
from Europeans. In 1896 his request for naturalization was refused. On 10 January 1896 Tagh 
was murdered while at prayer in the Coolgardie Mosque. On 13 November 1905 Faiz laid the 
foundation stone of the Perth Mosque. He later returned to India, and died in 1910.

pages.alt: Page 111. Case 8. Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 111 Mohamed Hasan Musakhan — also called Hassan Musa Khan — worked for the Mahomet brothers and wrote to Western Australian newspapers. On 24 April 1895 the Daily
pages.text:
Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 111
Mohamed Hasan Musakhan — also called Hassan Musa Khan — worked for the Mahomet 
brothers and wrote to Western Australian newspapers. On 24 April 1895 the Daily News printed 
his letter “The Anti-Asiatic League.” On 25 April 1895 The West Australian printed another 
letter from him.
Frederick Charles Burleigh Vosper, editor of the Coolgardie Miner, helped to found the Anti-
Asiatic League at Coolgardie in December 1894. On 16 June 1894 the Coolgardie Miner printed 
an editorial headed “The beginning of trouble.” It said the goldfield wanted camels, but not “the 
Asiatic driver.”
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test to keep many non-European people 
out. Cameleers already in Australia were often refused naturalization. Men who left to visit 
family could be refused re-entry if they failed the test or lacked the right certificate. In 1900 Faiz 
had permission from the Forrest government to import camels and drivers; a later government 
withdrew it. A 1902 select committee urged the Western Australian government to take 
responsibility for having granted permission and then withdrawn it.
Cameleers also worked on the Canning Stock Route in Western Australia. How that route was 
surveyed, and how water was found, involved Aboriginal people. That part of the story is flagged 
in the Teacher Note, and is not treated as settled on this page.
From the 1920s, motor trucks increasingly took the work that camel strings had done. Many 
cameleers left. Some stayed, married, and their families remain in Australia.

CASE 8 · YEAR 5–6 · THE ‘AFGHAN’ CAMELEERS · ASK
Three witnesses
Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used 
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness. 
Ask the same three questions of each.
Hassan Musa Khan, early 
twentieth century. Wikimedia 
Commons. Public domain.
Mohamed Hasan Musakhan
Clerk, writer and community spokesman · Worked for Faiz and Tagh Mahomet · 
Letters, 1895
A highly educated man from Karachi, he wrote to the newspapers to defend 
Afghan and Indian camel men, and to protest against the Anti-Asiatic 
League.
What they said
In the Daily News of 24 April 1895 he wrote that, from the addresses of Mr 
Vosper and others at the Anti-Asiatic League, “it is evident that the object 
of the league is to prevent the influx into W.A. of Chinese, Hindoos and 
Mohammedans in particular.” He went on: “It is the religious prejudice and 
not the colour prejudice that has prompted certain individuals to organise 
an association under the name of the so-called Anti-Asiatic League.” In The 
West Australian the next day, as later historians quote him, he pointed to 
the useful services of Afghan and Indian camel men on the goldfields, and 
said they would insist on their just demands as loyal subjects of Her 
Majesty.
Could they have seen it?
He was in Western Australia, he worked in the Mahomet brothers’ 
business, and he could read and write in English. He could describe how 
the League’s speeches sounded to the men he spoke for. He was a 
spokesman, not every cameleer. A later portrait cannot prove what he wrote 
in 1895. Whether “religious prejudice” or “colour prejudice” was the 
League’s main drive is something students can test against Vosper’s own 
words.
Why might they say it?
To answer a public campaign that wanted “Asiatic” men kept out, and to 
claim the rights of British subjects. A letter to a newspaper is evidence of a 
protest. It is also one man’s wording, written to persuade.
Source. Hassan Musa Khan, “The Anti-Asiatic League,” Daily News (Perth), 24 April 1895, p. 
3, as quoted in later historical work; and “To the Editor,” The West Australian, 25 April 1895, 
p. 6, as later historians quote it. The full citation, and a note that this file has not re-
transcribed every Trove line, is in the Teacher Note. The photograph is a real portrait, early 
twentieth century, Wikimedia Commons, public domain. No likeness has been invented.

Sir Thomas Elder, about 
1887, photograph by Duryea. 
State Library of South 
Australia. Public domain.
Sir Thomas Elder
Pastoralist and camel importer, South Australia · Died 1897
He brought camels into South Australia, and cameleers worked on his 
stations. Without those animals and those men, much inland carting would 
have waited for the truck.
What they said
In 1879 he wrote that he had imported camels from India in 1862, partly to 
help the exploration of the interior, and that the herd had grown from 110 
to 500 or 600. The record also shows that cameleers, including Faiz 
Mahomet, worked at his firm’s camel station at Hergott Springs. This file 
does not put extra words in his mouth about those men.
Could they have seen it?
He could speak about why he imported the camels, and about what they 
were for. He was an employer and an investor, writing years after 1862. He 
was not walking every camel pad, and he died in 1897, before the 
Immigration Restriction Act of 1901. He cannot settle, by himself, whether 
the men who worked the camels were welcomed.
Why might they say it?
To explain a business and exploration decision that made him famous. 
Praise for camels is not the same thing as a welcome for the men who drove 
them. Students can set his lecture beside the later refusals of naturalization.
Source. From a manuscript lecture of 1879, as quoted by the University of Adelaide: “The 
exploration of the interior is a subject which has engaged my attention for a number of 
years, and I had partly the furtherance of this object in view when in 1862 I imported camels 
from India, which have now become quite acclimatized in South Australia, and have 
increased in number from 110 to 500 or 600.” His employment of cameleers, including Faiz 
Mahomet at Hergott Springs, is documented in the Australian Dictionary of Biography entry 
for Faiz Mahomet. This card does not invent further sentences for Elder. The photograph is 
by Duryea, about 1887, State Library of South Australia B 11292, via Wikimedia Commons, 
public domain. No likeness has been invented.

pages.text:
Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 114
Frederick Vosper, published 
1897. Wikimedia Commons. 
Public domain.
Frederick C. B. Vosper
Editor, Coolgardie Miner · Founder, Anti-Asiatic League, 1894 · Died 1901
He used a goldfields newspaper, and a new league, to argue that Asian 
workers should be kept off the fields.
What they said
In the Coolgardie Miner of 16 June 1894 he printed: “We want camels, but 
we do not want the Asiatic driver. There are plenty of white men able to 
steer the ‘desert ships’ from the outer edges of civilization to any point.” 
The same editorial, as later historians quote it, called for “the protection of 
our Anglo-Saxon race” and used the camel command “ooshtah,” which it 
said meant “lay down,” adding, “we have no use for you at present.” The 
fuller wording, which uses still harsher racial language, is in the Teacher 
Note. It is not printed on this card.
Could they have seen it?
He was in Coolgardie, and he edited the paper. He could describe a 
campaign he was helping to lead. He could not speak for every miner, and 
he was not a cameleer. An editorial is not an eyewitness account of a single 
incident. It is a public argument.
Why might they say it?
To keep “Asiatic” workers off the goldfields, and to protect, as he saw it, 
white wages and a white colony. The League’s name tells you the frame. 
Students can ask whether “we want camels, but we do not want the Asiatic 
driver” is an economic argument, a racial one, or both.
Source. Editorial, “The beginning of trouble,” Coolgardie Miner, 16 June 1894, as quoted in

The typographic page is a constructed scene, written for this file. It is not a quotation, and not a 
named person’s diary. The handover line about tracks and whether the country opened to the 
cameleers is this file’s framing. What’s true sits in “What is agreed,” the witness cards, and this

Curriculum
The brief asked for an accurate AC9HS5 code. The lead code is AC9HS5K03: the role of a 
significant individual or group, including those who migrated to Australia, in the development 
of events in an Australian colony. The Immigration Restriction Act and citizenship after 
Federation also sit under AC9HS6K02. Both codes are used. There is no Year 5–6 “AC9HS9” 
code; that numbering belongs to later History courses, which use AC9HH.
Source conflicts, flagged
Faiz Mahomet’s arrival is given as about 1870 (ADB) and as 31 December 1865 (some later 
accounts). Musakhan’s year of death is given as 1939 in some accounts and 1945 in others. The 
25 April 1895 West Australian wording is taken from later historical quotation, not from a fresh 
Trove transcription by this file; it should be checked if a teacher has the page. The “Sons of God” 
sentence sometimes attached to Faiz after the Coolgardie food shortage of 1893 is cited to Brian 
Willis (1992) in later retellings. This file has not verified that sentence in a primary source, and 
does not use it on student pages.
First Nations, and consultation
Draft, pending consultation. The Canning Stock Route, and marriages with Aboriginal women, 
are First Nations histories as well as cameleer histories. Teach with AIATSIS guidance. Do not 
treat the stock-route survey and well-sinking as a colourful extra. The student pages name the 
route and leave the harm in this note, on purpose.

Most of the cameleers were Muslim. Teach the faith with respect. The word “Afghan” is 
explained as a settler label. Vosper’s editorial uses racist language; the harshest sentence is kept 
for this note and for Super Sleuths, so Year 5–6 teachers can decide how to handle it.

WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1889–1902 RECORDS, AND AFTER
Sir Henry Parkes, five times Premier of New South Wales, spoke at a banquet in the School of Arts at 
Tenterfield on 24 October 1889. He called for an Australian government and an Australian parliament, 
and for a convention to draw up a constitution. The next morning, The Sydney Morning Herald printed a 
long report of the speech, mostly in reported speech — “he said,” “they had to consider” — not as a word-
for-word script in the first person.
On 6 February 1890, at a banquet in Melbourne for the Australasian Federation Conference, Parkes 
responded to the toast “A United Australasia.” The line most often remembered from that night is: “The 
crimson thread of kinship runs through us all.” In the same speech he spoke of a shared British origin. 
That “us” did not include everyone who lived on this continent.
Parkes died in Sydney on 27 April 1896. He did not see 1 January 1901, when the Commonwealth of 
Australia came into being at a ceremony in Centennial Park, Sydney. Edmund Barton became the first 
Prime Minister.
The Constitution had been agreed to in referendums, colony by colony, in 1898, 1899 and 1900, and then 
passed by the British Parliament. Who could vote in those referendums was not the same in every colony. 
In most colonies the voters were adult men. Women could already vote in South Australia, and, from 1899, 
in Western Australia, and they could take part in the later referendums there. Aboriginal people were not 
treated the same way in every colony. In Western Australia, and in Queensland, most Aboriginal people 
were kept off the roll. The picture is more complicated in some other colonies, and this file does not 
pretend it was simple.
The Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said two things that matter for this case. Section 127 said that, in 
reckoning the numbers of the people, “aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi), the “race 
power,” gave the Commonwealth Parliament power to make special laws for “the people of any race, other 
than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both provisions were later changed, in 1967. This file does not treat 
1967 as the end of the story.
On 12 June 1902 the Commonwealth Franchise Act became law. It gave the federal vote to men and 
women who were twenty-one or over, British subjects, resident, and on the roll — and then shut many 
people out. It said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the Islands of the Pacific except New 
Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral Roll unless so entitled under section 
forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41, and how it was later read, is still argued over. In 1901 the new 
Parliament also passed the Immigration Restriction Act, which used a dictation test to keep many people 
out.
New Zealand did not join the Commonwealth. Parkes had spoken of “Australasia” at the 1890 banquet; the 
nation that began in 1901 was the six Australian colonies.
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.

Edmund Barton
Federation campaigner · First Prime Minister, 1 January 1901 · Died 1920
He helped to carry the federal cause after Parkes died, and he was sworn in as the first 
Prime Minister at Centennial Park.
Source. The Ashfield gathering of 1897 is the usual source for his best-known line about a nation and a 
continent. He was there in 1897, four years before the ceremony of 1 January 1901. The photograph is from 
1898, National Library of Australia, and is in the public domain in Australia (taken before 1 January 1955). 
No likeness has been invented.
What they said. At a federation rally in Ashfield, in 1897, he is recorded as saying: “For 
the first time in history, we have a nation for a continent and a continent for a nation.” That 
line is often later attached to 1 January 1901. This file keeps it in 1897, where the record 
places it. In 1901 he became the first Prime Minister of the new Commonwealth.
Could they really have seen it? He was a leading federalist, and he was at the centre of the 
campaign and of the first government. He could speak about the nation he wanted. He could not, 
from Ashfield in 1897, have seen the ceremony of 1901, or the Franchise Act of 1902. He also 
could not speak for people who were given no vote, and no place in the count.
Why might they say it? To persuade people to vote yes, and to describe the kind of nation the 
campaigns were offering. A phrase about “a nation for a continent” is a claim about land and 
people. Students can ask who was included in that “we.”

Rose Scott
New South Wales suffragist · Founding president, Women’s Political Educational 
League, 1902 · Died 1925
She spent years campaigning for women to have a say in the laws that governed them. The 
new federal vote, when it came, did not include everyone.
Source. Her public work is documented in contemporary records and in later biographical accounts. This 
card does not invent a speech for her, and it does not put words in quotation marks that this file has not 
checked word for word. The photograph is a real studio portrait of July 1903, State Library of New South 
Wales, public domain (taken before 1 January 1955). No likeness has been invented.
What they said. This file does not invent her wording. What the 1902 Act itself said is not 
in doubt. It gave the federal vote to men and women who were twenty-one or over, British 
subjects, and on the roll. In the same Act it shut out any “aboriginal native of Australia Asia 
Africa or the Islands of the Pacific except New Zealand,” unless that person was already 
entitled under section 41 of the Constitution. Scott became founding president of the 
Women’s Political Educational League in the year that Act was passed.
Could they really have seen it? She was in New South Wales, and she had long worked for 
the women’s vote. She could see what the new federal law offered to women who were British 
subjects on the roll. She was not in every colony, and she was not the voice of the people the Act 
named in order to shut them out. A later photograph, from July 1903, cannot prove what she 
said in 1901.
Why might they say it? Suffragists had fought for women to be included. The federal law that 
followed included many women, and still left many people out. Students can set her campaign 
beside the words of the Act, and ask whose say the new nation was built on.

Mei Quong Tart
Chinese-Australian merchant and community figure, Sydney · Died 1903
A well-known Sydney merchant, he wrote to the first Prime Minister about how the new 
Commonwealth’s immigration law was affecting Chinese people.
Source. The National Archives of Australia holds a letter from Quong Tart to Edmund Barton, dated 8 
January 1903, about the Immigration Restriction Act 1901 — including domicile certificates, the education 
test, and state deposits. This card summarises what that archive record is, and does not invent sentences 
from a letter this file has not transcribed word for word. The photograph is a real portrait of about 1900, 
National Library of Australia, public domain (taken before 1 January 1955). No likeness has been invented.
What they said. On 8 January 1903, two years after the Commonwealth began, he wrote 
to Prime Minister Barton about the way the Immigration Restriction Act was being used 
against Chinese people. The Archives describe the letter as dealing with domicile 
certificates, the education test, and state deposits. The education test — the dictation test — 
was the device the 1901 Act used to keep many people out, without always naming a race in 
the test itself.
Could they really have seen it? He lived in Sydney, and he had standing in both Chinese and 
European circles. He could describe what the new law was doing to people he knew. He wrote 
after 1901, not at the Centennial Park ceremony, and not as a voter who had been invited to help 
write the Constitution. He also cannot be made to stand in for Aboriginal people, whose 
exclusion was written into other clauses.
Why might they say it? To ask the first Prime Minister to look at how the new nation’s law 
was falling on Chinese residents and travellers. A letter to Barton is evidence of a protest, and of 
who had to ask. It is not the same thing as having had a say in 1899 or 1900, when the 
Constitution was put to the referendums.

1. The Herald’s Parkes, not a rewritten “I”
The typographic page follows The Sydney Morning Herald of 25 October 1889, p. 8. The speech was 
given on 24 October. The Herald mostly used reported speech: “the great question which they had to 
consider was…” Later retellings, including some museum pages, turn this into first person (“we have 
to consider”). This file does not make that change.

2. “The crimson thread of kinship”
This line is from the Melbourne banquet of 6 February 1890, not from Tenterfield. In the same 
speech Parkes spoke of a shared British origin. “Us all” was a claim about kinship. It was not a claim 
that every person on this continent was included. Aboriginal people, and many Chinese-Australians, 
were outside that “thread” as Parkes drew it.
Question. If a speaker says “us all,” how can you tell who is meant?

3. He never saw it happen
Tenterfield, 24 October 1889. Melbourne banquet, 6 February 1890. Parkes died on 27 April 1896. 
The Commonwealth began on 1 January 1901. The handover line in this file is not a quotation from 
Parkes. It is this file’s plain statement of those dates.
Question. Why might it matter that the man later called the “Father of Federation” — a later title, not 
a name he gave himself on the typographic page — never saw the ceremony?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Who could vote in the referendums
The Constitution was put to voters in 1898, 1899 and 1900. The rules were not the same in every 
colony. Women could vote in South Australia, and, from 1899, in Western Australia. In most other

colonies the voters were adult men. Aboriginal people were widely excluded in Queensland and 
Western Australia. In some other colonies the picture is more complicated, and summaries 
sometimes flatten it. New South Wales’s 1898 result is often told as a majority that still failed a 
special threshold; later votes went the other way. Western Australia voted in 1900. New Zealand did 
not join.
Question. Why is “the people voted for Federation” too simple a sentence?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Section 127, and the race power
Section 127 of the Constitution, as it stood in 1901, said that in reckoning the numbers of the people, 
“aboriginal natives shall not be counted.” Section 51(xxvi) gave the Commonwealth power to make 
special laws for “the people of any race, other than the aboriginal race in any State.” Both were 
changed in 1967. This file does not treat those later changes as if they cancelled the 1901 record, or as 
if they ended every question about who counts.
Question. What is the difference between not being counted, and not being allowed to vote?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. The 1902 Franchise Act, and section 41
The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902, assented to on 12 June, gave the federal vote to men and 
women who met its tests — and then said: “No aboriginal native of Australia Asia Africa or the 
Islands of the Pacific except New Zealand shall be entitled to have his name placed on an Electoral 
Roll unless so entitled under section forty-one of the Constitution.” Section 41 is a difficult clause. 
Later governments and courts often read it narrowly. This file flags that dispute rather than settling 
it.
Question. Why might a law that is remembered for giving women the federal vote also be a record of 
who was shut out?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
7. Quong Tart’s letter, and the dictation test
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test to keep many people out. On 8 January 
1903 Quong Tart wrote to Barton about how that law was affecting Chinese people. The National 
Archives of Australia describes the letter; this file has not printed a word-for-word extract, because it 
has not checked a full transcription against the original in this build. In 1894, Sir Henry Parkes had 
written a letter of introduction for Quong Tart, praising his “energy and integrity.” Parkes’s “crimson 
thread” and Parkes’s respect for one Chinese-Australian merchant can both be in the record.

“For the first time in history, we have a nation for a continent and a continent for a nation” is

CASE 9 · YEAR 6 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
Draft, pending consultation. This case asks who was left out of the new nation, including 
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. Teach it with care. Follow AIATSIS guidance, and 
do not treat this file as a finished account of First Nations experience. The user’s name is kept 
off the student pages and off the app.
What is quoted, and what is framing
The typographic page is not a facsimile of a newspaper, and it is not a diary. It is a typographic 
setting of verified wording. The Tenterfield lines are taken from The Sydney Morning Herald, 
25 October 1889, p. 8, which reported the banquet speech of 24 October. The Herald used 
reported speech. This file keeps “they had to consider,” “had done,” “could bring about,” and 
“He believed that the time had come.” It does not rewrite those lines as “I” or “we.” Some later 
museum and classroom pages do make that change. The Teacher Note flags them, rather than 
following them.
The last line on the typographic page, “The crimson thread of kinship runs through us all,” is 
from Parkes’s response to the toast “A United Australasia” at the Federation Conference 
banquet in Queen’s Hall, Parliament House, Melbourne, on 6 February 1890. It is not from 
Tenterfield. It is one of the most widely attested sentences in the Federation story. Teachers 
should still check a contemporary report (The Argus or The Age, 7 February 1890, or a careful 
later printing) beside this page.
“He never saw it happen” is this file’s handover. It is not a quotation from Parkes. The dates 
under it are not in dispute: he died on 27 April 1896; the Commonwealth began on 1 January 
1901. The file does not invent a Centennial Park scene in his voice, or a child’s invented diary of 
that morning, on the student pages.
Care, and conflicts this file will not settle
Who could vote in each referendum is not a single rule. Women voted in South Australia, and in 
Western Australia from 1899. Aboriginal voting was restricted or denied in Queensland and 
Western Australia; elsewhere the picture is more complicated, and secondary summaries 
sometimes flatten it. Section 41 of the Constitution, and how it was later applied to people 
already on a state roll, is still argued over. The 1902 Act’s exclusion is quoted from the Act itself 
(assented 12 June 1902). “Father of Federation” is a later title. Barton’s “nation for a continent” 
line is kept at Ashfield, 1897, not moved to 1 January 1901. This file summarises Quong Tart’s 8 
January 1903 letter from the National Archives’ description; it does not print a word-for-word 
extract, because a full checked transcription of that letter was not in hand for this build. 
Parkes’s 1 March 1894 letter of introduction for Quong Tart is in the State Library of New South 
Wales papers.

A notebook, opened more than a century later
New Year’s Day, 1915 — and now
They packed for a picnic.
That’s the bit I can’t get past. Ore wagons with benches in them. 
Sandwiches. About a thousand people going to Silverton, and a 
girl my age on the train, sitting next to someone she liked.
They saw an ice-cream cart by the line, and a flag, and two men. 
Some of them thought the shots were for the new year. Then the 
shots weren’t.
Four people were killed. Seven were hurt. That night a crowd 
burned the German Club, and the police had to stand in front of a 
mosque so the same crowd wouldn’t go there next.
I keep looking for a clean reason. The notes they left 
don’t give me one I can live with. Neither does what the 
town did after.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
This file includes a shooting in which four people were killed, and a riot that night against German 
and Muslim residents. Teach the violence with care. The opening notebook is written for this file; 
what’s true sits in the teacher notes. A note for teachers is at the end of the case.
CASE 10 · YEAR 9 · THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · READ
The Battle of Broken Hill, 1 January 1915
Why did they do it, and was the backlash fair?
What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.
On the morning of 1 January 1915, a picnic train left Broken Hill for Silverton for the annual 
Manchester Unity Oddfellows picnic. The Barrier Miner, printed the same day, said the train left 
Sulphide-street station at 10 a.m., and that it consisted of two brake vans and 40 ore trucks, 
“with a freight of some 1200 picnickers on board.” Some later accounts say 41 carriages. This file 
records both, and does not choose.
Beside the line, an ice-cream cart was flying a small red flag with a white crescent and star — the 
Ottoman (Turkish) flag. Two men, later named as Gool Badsha Mahomed (the spelling of his 
name varies) and Mullah Abdullah, fired on the train. Four people were killed: Alma Priscilla 
Cowie, aged 17, a passenger; William John Shaw, aged 46, a passenger; Alfred Millard, who was 
riding a bicycle beside the line (his middle name is given as Elton in the NSW Police Gazette and 
some official reports, and as Elvin in some later accounts); and James Craig, aged 69, who was 
in his yard and was hit during the later gunfight, not on the train. Seven other people were 
wounded, including Constable Robert Mills.
Police, military men under Lieutenant Resch, and armed civilians pursued the two men to a 
quartz outcrop later known as White Rocks. Both men were shot. Abdullah was found dead. 
Gool was badly wounded and died in hospital. Sources disagree on how long the gunfight lasted: 
about 40 minutes in one later museum account; almost two hours in others.
Notes were found. Contemporary reports and later summaries do not all give the same wording. 
They agree that the notes linked the attack to the Ottoman Sultan and to the writers’ faith, and
