pages.text:
Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 139
that Abdullah’s note also named a grudge against Chief Sanitary Inspector Cornelius Brosnan, 
who had prosecuted him for slaughtering animals away from the licensed abattoir. Gool’s note is 
widely reported to have been written for him by Abdullah, because Gool was illiterate. This file 
has not inspected the original notes.
That night a crowd in Broken Hill attacked and set fire to the German Club. Police later 
described the building as “maliciously set fire to and destroyed.” The club’s trustees offered a 
reward of £25; the state government matched it. Police and military were also sent to the North 
Camel Camp and the mosque, after a crowd moved in that direction. Officers later returned to 
the mosque because they had entered it without removing their boots.
Local Muslim residents were threatened. The two men’s bodies were buried by police at an 
undisclosed place. A coronial inquest on the four victims opened, was adjourned, and was held 
on 7 January 1915; an inquiry into the deaths of Gool and Abdullah followed the next day. The 
coroner found that the four had died from gunshot wounds feloniously inflicted by the two men, 
and that the shooting of the two men was justifiable.
Gool and Abdullah were Muslim men who had lived at the cameleers’ camp. Police records and 
newspapers did not agree on their nationality, and often called them Turks because of the flag. 
Later accounts describe Abdullah as probably from Afghanistan or a neighbouring region, 
literate in Dari, and Gool as an Afridi man from the Tirah region who had earlier served in the 
Ottoman army and, by 1915, sold ice-cream in Broken Hill. The Ottoman Empire had entered 
the war against Britain in late October 1914.

Three witnesses
Each witness is a real person, or a real set of words from the record. A period portrait is used 
where one exists and is free to reuse. Otherwise you will see a plain silhouette, not a likeness. 
Ask the same three questions of each.
A silhouette, not a likeness. 
No period portrait of M. 
Kenny has been located for 
this file.
M. Kenny
Passenger on the picnic train · Electrician on the water-supply works · Named 
in The Barrier Miner, 1 January 1915
A named passenger, close enough to see the cart, the flag, and the rifles, 
whose account was printed the day it happened.
What they said
The Barrier Miner reported that the two men “attracted the attention of Mr. 
M. Kenny, who was a passenger on the train.” Kenny, “engaged on the 
water supply works in the capacity of electrician, thought at first that there 
most be something wrong with the main, and that these men were 
attending to the damage. He then saw that they had rifles in their hands, 
pointed at the train, and almost simultaneously he saw and heard the rifles 
fired.” The paper said the firing continued while the train passed, “20 or 30 
shots being fired in all,” and that the men “could be plainly seen to be either 
Turks or Afghans.”
Could they have seen it?
He was on the train, close to the water main and the cart. He could see what 
was in front of him that morning. He could not see the notes in the men’s 
belts, or what happened at the German Club that night, or why the two men 
had come. A newspaper report, even a same-day one, is still a reporter’s 
wording of what Kenny said.
Why might they say it?
He was asked, or he offered, an eyewitness account of a public shock. A 
man who first thought of a broken water main is useful, because it shows 
how ordinary the scene looked until it wasn’t. It is still one pair of eyes, 
from one wagon, printed in a town already reaching for the word “Turks.”
Source. The Barrier Miner (Broken Hill), 1 January 1915, “War in Broken Hill,” as reprinted 
from the same-day report. This card follows that report’s wording, and does not add details 
from later retellings. No period portrait of M. Kenny has been located for this file. The image 
is a silhouette, not a likeness.

The notes left by Gool Badsha Mahomed and 
Mullah Abdullah
Written statements found after the shooting · 1 January 1915 · Wording differs 
between reports
The two men’s own last words, as newspapers and later writers reported 
them. They are evidence. They are also translations, and they do not all 
match.
What they said
Reports agree that the notes tied the attack to the Ottoman Sultan and to 
the writers’ faith. One widely quoted fragment from Gool’s note is: “I must 
kill you and give my life for my faith.” Some later accounts give a longer 
wording, including a claim to hold the Sultan’s order. Abdullah’s note, as 
later summarised, said he was dying for his faith and in obedience to the 
Sultan, “but owing to my grudge against Chief Sanitary Inspector Brosnan, 
it was my intention to kill him first.” Brosnan had prosecuted him for 
slaughtering animals away from the licensed abattoir, which Abdullah used 
so that the meat would be halal. William John Shaw, who died on the train, 
also worked in the sanitary department; he is not the man named in the 
note.
Could they have seen it?
They could write, or have written, what they wanted people to believe about 
their motives. They could not be cross-examined. A translation can shift a 
sentence. A note that mentions both a holy war and a local grudge does not 
tell you which reason, if either, came first. Later claims that a Sultan’s letter 
was forged, or that the flag was planted, are disputed, and are flagged in 
Super Sleuths.
Why might they say it?
To leave a reason behind, and to place the killing inside a war and a faith — 
and, in Abdullah’s case, inside a quarrel with an inspector. A last note can 
be a confession, a claim, or a justification. It cannot, by itself, tell you 
whether the town’s answer that night was fair.
Source. Contemporary newspaper reports and later summaries of the notes, including 
accounts that Gool’s note was written for him by Abdullah. Wording is not identical across 
sources. This card uses short, widely reported fragments, and does not stitch them into a 
single invented letter. This file has not inspected the original notes held in the archives. No 
death photographs are used. The image is a silhouette, not a likeness of either man.

Inspector Miller is used in

Inspector Miller, and the police record of that 
night
Broken Hill police · The German Club, the camel camp, and the inquest · 
January 1915
The official response after the shooting: a pursuit, a fire, a guard on a 
mosque, and a coroner’s finding.
What they said
The Barrier Miner said Inspector Miller sent police to the scene as soon as 
the alarm was telephoned in. That night, after a crowd set fire to the 
German Club, police and military were sent to the mosque at the North 
Camel Camp “to preserve order,” because they “feared a repetition of the 
proceedings” at the club. A crowd of some hundreds was held off. Days 
later, Inspector Miller and Captain Hardie visited the mosque again, after 
officers had entered it without removing their boots. The coroner found the 
four deaths felonious, and the shooting of Gool and Abdullah justifiable. 
The government matched a reward for information about the burning of 
the club, as a statement against vigilantism.
Could they have seen it?
Miller could describe what his men were sent to do, and what they found. 
He was not on the picnic train when the first shots were fired, and he could 
not see inside every part of a night crowd. A police report, and a coroner’s 
finding, are official. They are also frames: they can tell you that the club was 
burned, and still leave open how fair the town’s anger was.
Why might they say it?
To keep order, to show that the two men were stopped, and to show — after 
the fire — that a riot would not be treated as nothing. Officials had reasons 
to calm a town and to defend their own conduct. Students can set the guard 
on the mosque beside the fact that a crowd had already burned a building, 
and beside the later protest when police entered the mosque in boots.
Source. The Barrier Miner, 1 January 1915 and following days, as reported and later 
summarised, including the police description of the German Club as “maliciously set fire to 
and destroyed,” the reward offered by the club’s trustees and matched by the state, the guard 
on the North Camel Camp and mosque, and the later conciliatory visit after officers had 
entered the mosque in boots. The coronial findings of 7–8 January 1915 are reported in later 
official and newspaper accounts, including the NSW Police Gazette, 17 February 1915. No 
period portrait of Inspector Miller is used here. The image is a silhouette, not a likeness.

My finding
The three witness cards are M. Kenny, the notes the two men left, and the police record of that night. Further 
people — including Walhanna Asson, Cornelius Brosnan, and the local Muslim community — are in Super Sleuths.
You have a constructed notebook, a short agreed file, and three witnesses. The opening page is 
not a 1915 diary. Say what you think the records can prove about why the two men fired, and 
whether the town’s answer that night was fair. “We can’t know” is an honest finding when the 
notes conflict, or when the record of the riot is thinner than the record of the shooting. Do not 
invent what the sources do not say. Treat the dead, and the living families of this story, with 
care.
Why did they do it, and was the backlash fair?
Circle one: They did it as an act of war for the Ottoman Sultan · They did it because of a local grudge 
and years of being shut out · Both of those things were tangled together, and we can’t separate them 
cleanly · The backlash was not fair, even if the shooting was a crime · We can’t know, from this 
file, all of why they did it, or how far the town’s anger spread · Another finding, written below
MY FINDING
My finding. ________________________________________________
______________________________________________________________
The one piece of evidence that most changed my mind. ________
______________________________________________________________
What I still can’t know. ___________________________________
______________________________________________________________
Why it still matters
The “Battle of Broken Hill” is still told as a curiosity of the First World War on Australian soil, 
and sometimes as if it were simple. The file is open because the notes do not all say the same 
thing, because a picnic train is not a battlefield, and because the night that followed — a burned 
club, a guarded mosque, a secret burial — is part of the same case. How a town answers a crime, 
and who it answers it upon, still matters.

4. James Craig was not on the train
Three people were killed in the attack on the train and the pipe track: Alma Cowie, William Shaw, 
and Alfred Millard. James Craig was in his yard, about a hundred yards from the Cable Hotel, and 
was hit during the later gunfight. A stepdaughter urged him to come inside. Treating all four deaths 
as if they happened in the ore wagons flattens the day.
Question. Why does it matter, for a finding, where each of the four was when they were hit?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Walhanna Asson, and the camel camp
Walhanna Asson, a Punjabi-speaking camel-owner from Peshawar, carried water to a wounded 
constable while under fire, and was himself nearly shot by late-comers who took him for “one of the 
enemy” until police protected him. That night a crowd moved on the mosque. Officers later went back 
because they had entered it in boots. Local Muslims protested when a gravedigger began two graves 
in their cemetery for the two attackers. The backlash did not fall only on a club that happened to be 
German.
Question. If you are asked whether the backlash was fair, whose evidence belongs in the answer — 
the burned club, the guarded mosque, Asson, or all of them?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
6. Were “all Germans” already interned?
Some later retellings say the German Club stood empty because every German in Australia had 
already been interned. That is too strong for 1 January 1915. Internment of “enemy aliens” happened 
during the war, and it was not a single clean sweep on one day. The club was burned. German 
residents were threatened. How many people were in the club that night, and how internment later 
widened, should be checked, not assumed.

CASE 10 · YEAR 9 · THE BATTLE OF BROKEN HILL, 1915 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page. The user’s name is kept off the student pages and off 
the app.
What’s true about the opener
The typographic page is a constructed Year 10 student notebook, written for this file, in an 
angsty voice. It is not a 1915 diary and not the voice of a named historical person. “A girl my 
age” is Alma Priscilla Cowie, 17; the opener does not invent her thoughts or last words. Violence 
is named, not described in graphic detail. No death photographs are used anywhere in the file.
Curriculum
The brief asked for an accurate AC9HS9 code. There is no AC9HS9. Year 9 History uses 
AC9HH9 codes. The lead code is AC9HH9K11: the effects of the First World War on Australian 
society. The shooting happened on Australian soil in January 1915, after the Ottoman Empire 
had entered the war; the aftermath includes a riot, a burned German Club, and the treatment of 
a local Muslim community. AC9HH9K09 (places Australians fought) is not used as the lead, 
because this was not a campaign overseas.
Source conflicts, flagged
Alma / Elma Cowie; Alfred Elton / Elvin Millard; 40 trucks / 41 carriages; “some 1200” 
picnickers; gunfight of about 40 minutes / almost two hours; varied spellings of Gool Badsha 
Mahomed (Gool, Goul, Mahomed, Mohammed, Mahommed). Translations of the notes do not 
all match. Later “planted flag” / forged letter claims are not treated as agreed. Overstatements 
that “every German” had already been interned are flagged. Shaw worked in the sanitary 
department; the man named in Abdullah’s note is Inspector Brosnan, not Shaw.
Religion, race, and care
Gool and Abdullah were Muslim. The local cameleer community was not the same as the two 
men. Teach the faith, and the camp, with respect. Do not let the word “Turk,” which 1915 papers 
used because of the flag, erase that uncertainty. Living families, including descendants of 
victims and of the camel camp, deserve legal and ethical care even though the principals are 
long dead. Year 9–10 students can hold two things at once: the killing of civilians was a crime, 
and a riot against other people’s club, camp and mosque still has to be judged.
Country
Broken Hill is on Wilyakali Country. This file does not tell a First Nations history of the event, 
and does not invent one. A deeper local treatment would need consultation. The student pages 
do not pretend otherwise.

A NOTE BEFORE YOU READ
This file is about a hospital ship sunk in wartime, with heavy loss of life. It includes named dead, 
injured survivors, and a disputed attribution. Teach it with care for the dead and for their families. 
The opening notebook is written for this file; what’s true sits in the teacher notes. A note for teachers 
is at the end of the case.
CASE 11 · YEAR 10 · SISTER ELLEN SAVAGE AND THE HOSPITAL SHIP 
CENTAUR, 1943 · READ
Sister Ellen Savage and the hospital ship Centaur, 
1943
What can the records prove about who sank a marked hospital ship, and 
whether it was legitimately protected?
What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.
On 14 May 1943, shortly after 4 a.m., the 2/3rd Australian Hospital Ship Centaur was sunk off 
the Queensland coast. She had left Sydney unescorted on 12 May, bound north, carrying her 
crew and medical staff, including members of the 2/12th Field Ambulance, and no patients. The 
Australian War Memorial places the sinking south of Moreton Island; an older Memorial 
encyclopedia entry gave a position of about 27°17′ S, 153°58′ E, about 50 miles east-north-east 
of Brisbane. Some later accounts give the time as 4.10 a.m. This file uses the Memorial’s 
wording, “shortly after 4 am,” and notes the variation.
A contemporary correction, reported on 20 May 1943, said that a further check by Australian 
Army and Navy authorities had revised an earlier figure of 363 people on board down to 332, 
“with a corresponding diminution in casualties.” The Australian War Memorial uses the figures 
332 on board and 64 survivors (268 people died). Some later summaries give 322 on board. This 
file uses the Memorial’s 332 and 64, and records that later figures sometimes differ. Twelve 
nursing sisters were on board. Only Sister Ellen Savage, Australian Army Nursing Service, 
survived.
Period photographs, including Australian War Memorial 302796, a port-side view taken in 
Sydney in 1943 and now in the public domain, show a white hull, a green band, and prominent 
red crosses on the hull, the funnel, and the stern, with another cross lying horizontally on the

pages.text:
Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 156
after deckhouse. The Memorial has described the ship as appropriately lit and marked as a 
hospital ship. One Memorial exhibition page calls her “brightly-lit” at the time she was hit. A 
photograph of the ship in harbour, and a later official wording about lights, do not by themselves 
prove what a submarine commander could see at night.
The sinking was very rapid. One Memorial article says the ship sank in about three minutes. 
Some survivors, quoted in a 20 May 1943 newspaper report, said ballast in her bottom helped to 
send her under “in a few seconds.” Seaman Martin Pash, as quoted by the Australian War 
Memorial, said the Centaur “just went straight down.” The 64 survivors spent about a day and a 
half in the water and on rafts before they were spotted by a RAAF aircraft and taken off by the 
United States destroyer USS Mugford, as recorded by the Memorial.
Sister Ellen Savage, service number NFX.76584, was the only nurse to survive. The London 
Gazette of 25 August 1944 recorded the award of the George Medal to “Sister (Miss) Ellen 
Savage, NFX.76584, Australian Army Nursing Service,” “in recognition of conspicuous gallantry 
in carrying out hazardous work in a very brave manner.” Two days after the rescue she was 
interviewed in hospital by Mervyn Weston; that interview was printed in the Newcastle Morning 
Herald and Miners’ Advocate, 19 May 1943, p. 2. The paper called her Eleanor; other reports 
used Nellie. The Gazette names her Ellen Savage.
The Australian Government sent an official protest to Japan through Switzerland. The Advocate 
(Burnie), 20 May 1943, reported that Prime Minister John Curtin “stated emphatically” that all 
those on board were non-combatants, “members of a medical corps,” and that the Army legal 
branch held the protection of Army medical personnel on a hospital ship was “clearly expressed 
in the Geneva and Hague conventions,” and was not lost because there were no sick or wounded 
on board. The Australian War Memorial later summarised that Japan “did not acknowledge 
responsibility for the incident for many years,” and that “the War Crimes Tribunal could not 
identify the responsible submarine.” A later Japanese official war history, as summarised by the 
Memorial, attributed the sinking to submarine I-177 under Lieutenant Commander Nakagawa. 
This file records both summaries, and does not treat the later official history as a courtroom 
finding.

May 1943. AWM 044428.

Sister Ellen Savage, AANS
The only nursing sister to survive · Interviewed two days after the rescue · 
Awarded the George Medal
A named survivor, speaking in hospital in May 1943, about the explosion, 
her friend, the water, and the raft.
What they said
Savage said her best friend, Sister King, was in the next cabin, and that she 
heard her shout, “Quick, Savage, up on deck.” They had often talked about 
what they would do if they were ever torpedoed. Sister King could not 
swim, “and it had been agreed that I should crocodile her — that is, take her 
across my shoulders — if we ever finished in the water.” “So, after meeting 
on deck, we jumped into the water together. Sister King was apparently 
killed by debris, for I never saw her again. It was then that I apparently 
injured my side, but I did not realise it at the time. I am a strong swimmer, 
and immediately struck away from the ship when I realised that Sister King 
had disappeared.” She said she climbed onto a section of the deck-house 
with Robert Westwood, “the 15-year-old cabin boy, who had burns,” and 
that they worked their way to two rafts “on which nearly 20 men were 
huddling.” A man gave her a greatcoat. “I gave Westwood what attention I 
could, and sheltered him against me with the greatcoat. This great coat 
undoubtedly saved my life.”
Could they have seen it?
She was on the ship when it was hit, and in the water afterwards. She could 
speak about what she heard, what she did, and whom she could no longer 
find. She could not see who fired the torpedo, or from which submarine, or 
what that person could see of the markings and the lights. She was injured, 
newly rescued, and speaking to a reporter. A newspaper interview is still a 
reporter’s wording of what she said. Accounts of her injuries are not 
identical across the 19 May article and later Memorial quotations.
Why might they say it?
She was asked, two days after the rescue, to say what had happened. She 
named her friend, the plan they had made, a boy she tried to help, and a 
coat that kept her alive. That is evidence of the sinking as a person lived it. 
It is not evidence of who fired, or of whether the ship’s markings could be 
seen from a submarine at night.
Source. “Nurse Heroine of Lost Ship Trained at Newcastle,” Newcastle Morning Herald and 
Miners’ Advocate, 19 May 1943, p. 2, http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article140459114. 
Interview by Mervyn Weston, two days after the rescue. The paper names her Eleanor; the 
London Gazette names her Ellen Savage, NFX.76584. Quotations are from that interview; 
obvious OCR errors have been corrected. Check the original page. The portrait is AWM 
044428, May 1943, at Greenslopes. That photograph is a later interview than Weston’s. 
Copyright expired — public domain.

Hospital ship Centaur, 
Sydney, 1943. AWM 302796. 
Copyright expired — public 
domain.
The hospital ship Centaur, as marked
2/3rd Australian Hospital Ship · Photographed in Sydney, 1943 · Officially 
described as marked and lit
The ship herself, speaking through a 1943 photograph and through official 
descriptions of her markings and lights.
What they said
The photograph shows a white hospital ship with a dark band along the hull 
and large crosses painted on her side. The Memorial’s caption names the 
band as green, and the crosses as red, and points to further crosses on the 
funnel, the stern, and the after deckhouse. The Memorial has said the ship 
“had been appropriately lit and marked to indicate that it was a hospital 
ship,” and that her sinking “was regarded as an atrocity.” In May 1943 the 
Army legal branch, as reported at the time, said the protection of Army 
medical personnel on a hospital ship was clearly expressed in the Geneva 
and Hague conventions, and was not lost because there were no sick or 
wounded on board.
Could they have seen it?
The camera, in Sydney harbour in 1943, could record how the ship was 
painted. It could not record how those markings looked from a submarine 
at sea, shortly after four in the morning, off the Queensland coast. An 
official description that the ship was lit and marked is strong evidence of 
how the Allies presented her. It is not, by itself, proof of what the person 
who fired could see, or of whether a notification of her identity — if one was 
sent, and if it arrived — had been read. Some later official and education 
accounts say her identification was passed to the International Committee 
of the Red Cross and to Japan in early February 1943. This file has not 
inspected the original notification papers, and does not treat that date as 
proved here.
Why might they say it?
Hospital ships were painted and lit so that, under the conventions, they 
could be recognised and left alone. After the sinking, official Australian 
voices had a reason to stress those markings, the lights, and the legal 
protection. That does not make the photograph untrue. It does mean 
students should ask what the markings can prove, and what they cannot.
Source. Australian War Memorial 302796, “Port side view of the hospital ship Centaur,” 
Sydney, 1943. The Memorial’s caption notes the red crosses and green lines on the hull, 
funnel, stern, and after deckhouse. Copyright expired — public domain. Official wording on 
lighting and marking is from the Australian War Memorial, including an exhibition page 
that calls the ship “brightly-lit” when she was hit. The Advocate (Burnie), 20 May 1943, 
records the Army legal branch on the Geneva and Hague conventions.

Lieutenant Commander

The official Japanese record, and Lieutenant 
Commander Hajime Nakagawa
A 1943 denial, a post-war investigation that did not identify the submarine, and a 
later official war history · Nakagawa, named in that later history, never 
commented on the Centaur
What was officially said, and not said, about who fired. This card is a 
record, not a confession.
What they said
In 1943, as the Memorial later put it, Japan did not accept responsibility. 
The Australian Government had already sent a protest through 
Switzerland. After the war, investigators, as summarised by the Memorial, 
could not identify the responsible submarine for a war-crimes prosecution. 
A later Japanese official war history, again as summarised by the Memorial, 
“makes clear that it was submarine I-177, under the command of Lt 
Commander Nakagawa who had sunk the Centaur.” Nakagawa himself left 
no statement on the Centaur for this file to quote. Some later naval histories 
have pointed to other Japanese submarines then off the Australian east 
coast, and have not all agreed on I-177.
Could they have seen it?
A government can deny, or later record, an attack it did not publicly accept 
at the time. A war-crimes investigation can fail to name a boat to a criminal 
standard, and still leave a suspicion on the file. A later official history can 
name a submarine and a commander without that naming having been 
tested in court. None of those records can show us the view from a 
periscope at night. Nakagawa could not be cross-examined, in this file, 
about what he saw, or whether he saw a hospital ship at all. He made no 
comment.
Why might they say it?
In 1943 a denial would have rejected an official Australian charge of an 
atrocity. A later official history, written long afterwards, may have been a 
historical accounting, not a confession in court. The honest position, from 
this file, is that the records name I-177 in a later official history, and do not 
name it in a completed prosecution.
Source. The Australian War Memorial encyclopedia entry “Centaur (Hospital ship),” as 
archived, summarises that Japan did not acknowledge responsibility for many years, that 
“the War Crimes Tribunal could not identify the responsible submarine,” and that a later 
Japanese official war history attributed the sinking to submarine I-177 under Lieutenant 
Commander Nakagawa. The same entry records that Nakagawa was convicted for firing on 
survivors of the British ship Chivalry — a different case, not a trial for the Centaur. This file 
has not inspected the war history or the investigation papers, and does not invent words for 
Nakagawa. He did not comment. The image is a silhouette, not a likeness.

Why it still matters
Hospital ships, and the rules meant to protect them, are still argued over when a marked ship is 
hit. The Centaur is commemorated in Australia as an atrocity; the question of who fired, and of 
what could be seen, has never been settled in a court. Families of the dead, and the wreck itself 
— found in 2009 and protected as a historic shipwreck and a memorial — are not a puzzle for 
students to solve. A careful finding will say what the 1943 records and the later official 
summaries can show, and what they cannot.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
1. What could be seen at night?
Allied official sources, including the Australian War Memorial, describe the Centaur as clearly 
marked and brightly lit. The 1943 photograph in this file shows the markings in harbour, in daylight. 
A submarine at periscope depth, shortly after 4 a.m., is a different point of view. Some later official 
and education accounts say her identification was passed to the International Committee of the Red 
Cross and to Japan in early February 1943. This file has not inspected those notification papers. A 
notification, even if it was sent and received, is not the same as a commander seeing a red cross in the 
dark.
Question. What can a photograph of a marked ship, an official wording about lights, and a claimed 
notification, each prove — and what can none of them prove about the view from a submarine?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
2. Who fired? The closed file and the later history
The Memorial’s encyclopedia entry records that post-war investigators could not identify the 
responsible submarine, and that a later Japanese official war history attributed the sinking to I-177 
under Lieutenant Commander Hajime Nakagawa. Nakagawa did not comment on the Centaur. He 
was convicted of other war crimes, for firing on survivors of another ship, not for this one. Some later 
naval histories have pointed to other Japanese submarines then off the east coast, and have not all 
agreed on I-177. This file does not treat the 1979 history, as reported by the Memorial, as a courtroom 
finding, and it does not invent a confession.
Question. If a later official history names a submarine, and a completed prosecution never did, what 
should a careful finding say?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
3. Cargo, rifles, and the conventions
After the sinking, and in later education materials, claims have been made about weapons and cargo:

that ambulance drivers tried to bring rifles and ammunition aboard; that the Master and the Chief 
Medical Officer questioned what the conventions allowed; that a search was made; that figures of 
about 52 rifles and 2,000 or 4,000 rounds appear in later retellings. Those figures do not all match, 
even in the same later materials. The Hague conventions allowed some arms for the maintenance of

rifles, if any, were in a hold, and it does not use an unsettled cargo claim to decide whether the ship 
was legitimately protected.
Question. Why might later writers argue about cargo and rifles, and why should a student keep those 
claims in amber until a named primary source is on the desk?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. Numbers that moved
In the week after the sinking, a reported official correction revised 363 people on board down to 332. 
The Memorial uses 332 and 64 survivors. Some later pages say 322. Figures for the 2/12th Field 
Ambulance also vary between later captions and later articles (for example, 14 survivors from “two 
hundred,” or 178 dead from 193). This file uses the Memorial’s 332 and 64, and the correction 
reported on 20 May 1943, and leaves the smaller disagreements in amber.
Question. Why might official numbers change in the first week, and why does a later disagreement 
about a unit total not undo the fact of the sinking?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. The wreck is a memorial, not a hunt
The wreck was found on 20 December 2009, about 30 nautical miles off the southern tip of Moreton 
Island, in deep water, and is now a protected historic shipwreck and a memorial. That discovery is 
part of the later history of the case. It is not the student question, and the site is not to be treated as a 
puzzle or a treasure hunt.
Question. Why might finding the wreck still leave the question of who fired, and of what could be 
seen, unsettled?

CASE 11 · YEAR 10 · SISTER ELLEN SAVAGE AND THE HOSPITAL SHIP 
CENTAUR, 1943 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher Note
This note is for the teacher. It is not a student page. The user’s name is kept off the student pages and off 
the app.
What’s true about the opener
The narrator is an invented Year 10 student, looking at a 1943 photograph and at a 1943 
interview. The photograph, the date, and Savage’s quoted words are in the opening scene. The 
Memorial’s wording about lights, the figures 332 and 64, the official protest, and the later 
conflict over I-177 sit in the case file, not in that scene; they are not invented. Seaman Martin 
Pash’s phrase “just went straight down” is used as quoted by the Australian War Memorial, not 
from a full interview text inspected for this file. Sister King and the cabin boy Robert Westwood 
are named because Savage named them in a published 1943 interview. Teach those names with 
care for the dead and for families.
What’s true about the exhibits
Four exhibits follow the opening scene. The casualty telegram is a reconstruction, clearly 
labelled, and is not a real telegram. It is addressed only to “the next of kin of a nursing sister,” 
not to a named family. The wording is modelled on official Army casualty telegrams of the 
period, including a Postmaster-General’s Department telegram in the Australian War 
Memorial’s papers of Reginald Walter Saunders, and the published military formula that begins 
“I regret to inform you” and conveys the sympathy of the Minister for the Army. The 
photograph is AWM 302796, Sydney, 1943, copyright expired — public domain. The 
handwritten caption on the back is the Memorial’s own catalogue wording, not an invented 
personal note. The radio bulletin is a reconstruction, not an original script or an original 
recording. Every sentence is taken from “Protest against sinking of Centaur,” Advocate 
(Burnie), 20 May 1943, p. 3, http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article68810542, including Curtin’s 
“stated emphatically,” “non-combatants,” and “members of a medical corps,” and the Army 
legal branch’s wording about the Geneva and Hague conventions. The audio in the app is a 
modern reading of that text, with a radio-style filter, and is labelled “Reconstruction, not 
original audio.” The newspaper extract is typeset from “Nurse Heroine of Lost Ship Trained at 
Newcastle,” Newcastle Morning Herald and Miners’ Advocate, 19 May 1943, p. 2, 
http://nla.gov.au/nla.news-article140459114. It is not a scan of the original page. The paper 
names her Eleanor; the London Gazette names her Ellen Savage, NFX.76584.

Two hundred and sixty-eight people died. Teach the sinking with care. Do not use photographs 
of human remains, or of bodies in the water, if they exist. Do not invent last words, panic, or 
suffering beyond what a named source actually says. Accounts of Savage’s injuries are not

identical; do not tidy them into one medical list. A 15-year-old cabin boy with burns is in the 
1943 interview. Handle that line carefully in a Year 10 classroom. The case is not a First Nations 
history as a whole, but a contemporary crew-survivor list printed on 20 May 1943 named E. M. 
Salt as a “Torres strait pilot.” This file does not examine that person’s story. If you take it 
further, do so with care, and with consultation if a Torres Strait Islander’s experience is taught 
in any depth.
I-177 and Nakagawa: do not settle a closed prosecution
Present the conflict, do not close it. The Memorial records that the war-crimes process could 
not identify the submarine, and that a later Japanese official war history named I-177 and 
Lieutenant Commander Hajime Nakagawa. Nakagawa did not comment on the Centaur. He 
died in 1991, so he is not a living person, but legal care still applies to how he is named: he was 
convicted of other crimes, not tried for this one. Do not print a student-facing finding that treats 
him as the settled offender. Some later naval histories have preferred other boats then off the 
east coast. If you use later press reports of a Japanese embassy comment after the 2009 wreck 
discovery, quote a named article, and do not treat a diplomatic wording as a verdict either way.
Markings, lights, notification, and cargo
Allied official sources say the ship was marked and lit. That is evidence. Students should still 
ask what a submarine commander could see, and what a claimed notification to Japan can 
actually prove. This file has not inspected original ICRC or Japanese notification papers, and so 
does not treat a February 1943 notification date as agreed fact. Cargo and rifle claims belong in 
Super Sleuths. Figures in later education materials conflict. Do not use an unsettled munitions 
story to decide the legal protection of a hospital ship, and do not invent a hidden cargo.
Names, numbers, and sources not used
1943 newspapers used Eleanor and Nellie as well as Ellen; the Gazette and the Memorial use 
Ellen Savage, NFX.76584. An early official total of 363 was corrected to 332 in May 1943. Prefer 
the Memorial’s 332 and 64, and flag later 322s. The AWM newsreel F00734, in which Savage 
was interviewed from a hospital bed, is not treated as public domain and is not used as a still in 
this file. A longer wording sometimes circulated as her George Medal “citation” has not been 
verified from the Gazette page inspected for this file; only the Gazette’s published award 
wording is used. A recommendation is held by the Memorial (RC02373) but is not quoted here.
Curriculum, placement, and publishing
This file is Case 11, Year 10, AC9HH10K02: “the places where Australians fought, and their 
perspectives and experiences during the Second World War, such as the fall of Singapore, 
prisoners of war (POWs), the Battle of Britain and Kokoda.” Whether that code is the best fit is 
still a teacher’s judgement; the official examples on the v9 page do not name the Centaur, but 
the case is a documented Australian experience of the war at sea, off the Queensland coast. The 
wreck is mentioned for the teacher and in Super Sleuths, not as the student hunt. The user’s

20 February 1965
Moree
Egg on my sleeve. I keep wiping it. Still there.
We came back. We had to. Last time they said the ban was off. We left. They put it 
back on. I don’t know why I thought a meeting would be enough.
The crowd was already at the pool. Pressing in. So hot I could hardly breathe. 
Someone spat. Then the tomatoes, the eggs. I have never been looked at like that.
I keep thinking we don’t live here. We’re from Sydney. We get on the bus. The 
children don’t.
The police said if we stayed it would get worse. We stayed. I wanted to go. I hate 
that I wanted to go.
Charlie wouldn’t move from the gate. They grabbed him. For a moment I couldn’t see 
the kids and I thought —
I thought I would be braver than this.
One of the children was knocked down. They were frightened. So was I. What a thing 
to come all this way and still be frightened.
They let them in, in the end. We went in too. For a minute it felt like winning. Then 
we had to walk to the bus in a single line and they were still throwing things and 
the windows kept getting hit.
A man at the bus said it quietly.
They’ll wait till you’re gone.
— on the bus

What happened in the towns the students visited, 
and who recorded it?
The Freedom Ride · New South Wales, February 1965
Draft, pending consultation with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially Moree and 
Walgett, and those they name, and with AIATSIS guidance.
Read the notebook page through to the last line. Then read what the 1965 file can agree on. After 
that, three people will be asked the same three questions.
CASE FILE: FREEDOM RIDE / 1965
Date of incident 12–26 February 1965 (Moree visits: 16 and 19–20 February)
Location Regional New South Wales, including Walgett and Moree
Status Unresolved contradictions · Draft, pending consultation
Key claims still disputed
– What actually changed in the towns, and for how long?
– Whose record should we trust — student diaries, local Aboriginal accounts, or the 1965 
newspapers and television?
– When was the Moree baths ban really lifted?
WHAT IS AGREED · FROM THE 1965 FILE, AND AFTER
Twenty-nine University of Sydney students left around midnight on 12 February 1965, as Student Action 
for Aborigines (SAFA). Charles Perkins, an Arrernte man, was president. Some left later and others joined.
They travelled through regional New South Wales for about two weeks, using surveys, pickets and 
cameras, and they kept diaries. Newspapers, radio and television reported the trip as it happened.
They went to Moree twice. On 16 February, Aboriginal children were at first refused the baths, then let in. 
That evening a public meeting voted 88 to 10 to remove the segregation clause.
After they left, the old 1955 rule was enforced again. They returned on 19–20 February. A hostile crowd 
met them at the pool. Eggs, tomatoes and stones were thrown. Children and students went in, then left 
that night through the crowd.
Local Aboriginal people were already campaigning in towns such as Walgett. The students met Harry Hall, 
president of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association, on 15 February.
The Moree baths rule used the period language of racial exclusion. The wording is in Super Sleuths, with a 
content note. The ban was not settled in a single day.
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.

CASE 12 · YEAR 10 · THE CASE
Three witnesses
The same three questions for each: What did they say they saw? · Could they really have seen it? · 
Why might they say it? Each has a plain silhouette and a name card. No likeness of a real person has 
been invented.
A NOTE ON THE LANGUAGE OF THE RECORDS
Some 1965 records, and some later interviews, use racist language. This file does not repeat slurs on 
the student pages. A short extract from the 1955 Moree baths rule is in Super Sleuths, clearly 
attributed, with a content note. It is not the language of this case file.
A silhouette, not a likeness.
Charles Perkins
Arrernte man · president of Student Action for Aborigines
A public statement after the ride, and a later account of the return to Moree.
Source. The line “The problem is out in the open now” is quoted by AIATSIS as said to about 200 people at 
the 1965 FCAATSI conference in Canberra. His book A Bastard Like Me (1975) describes the second Moree 
visit. Perkins died in 2000.
What they said. After the ride he told a national Aboriginal conference, “The problem is 
out in the open now.” Of the return to Moree he later wrote of a hostile crowd, and of 
getting the children in, then walking them back to the bus.
Could they really have seen it? He was on the bus from Sydney and at both Moree visits. He 
stood at the pool gate on the return. He was not a neutral observer: he led the group and wanted 
the colour bar broken and the story reported.
Why might they say it? To show that the ride had forced a public reckoning, and to keep 
pressure on the towns after the bus left. A book written years later is memory, not a 1965 diary.

Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 172
A silhouette, not a likeness.
Ann Curthoys
University of Sydney student on the bus · diarist
A diary kept on the trip, later published.
Source. Ann Curthoys, diary of the 1965 Freedom Ride, AIATSIS collection; published in Freedom Ride: A 
Freedom Rider Remembers (2002). Living — no dates given here.
What they said. Her diary of 16 February records a first visit to the Moree baths and an 
evening meeting that voted 88 to 10 to remove the segregation clause. Two days later she 
recorded that the old rule was being enforced again. Of the return she wrote that she had 
“never met such hostile, hate-filled people,” and that the hostility seemed aimed at the 
students as “university student intruders.” She noted eggs, tomatoes and stones, frightened 
children, and leaving in single file.
Could they really have seen it? She was on the bus and at both Moree visits. A diary written 
at the time is close to the events, but it is still one student’s view. She could not see everything in 
a crowd.
Why might they say it? She was keeping a record for herself, and later she published it as 
history. She was a city student on a protest, not a local resident.
What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________
A silhouette, not a likeness.
Harry Hall
President of the Walgett Aborigines’ Progressive Association
A local Aboriginal leader the students met in Walgett, before Moree.
Source. Named in accounts of the 1965 Walgett campaign, including the AIATSIS Freedom Ride page and 
reporting of the later 1965 colour-bar fights. He is deceased. This card is not a 1965 first-person diary. Do 
not confuse him with his son, who is living and is not this witness.
What they said. The 1965 record names him as president of the Walgett association, and 
as a person the students met when they reached the town on 15 February. Local 
campaigning against segregation was already underway. Later that year he asked Perkins 
and other activists to come back and help fight the colour bar at the Oasis Hotel.
Could they really have seen it? He lived in Walgett and had been campaigning there before 
the bus arrived. He was not at the Moree pool on 20 February. Much of what later family and 
community accounts add comes after 1965.
Why might they say it? To record that the ride did not start the fight in Walgett, and to get 
outside help when the colour bar was still in place after the bus had gone. Later memory is not 
the same thing as a 1965 statement.
What did they say they saw? ______________________________
Could they really have seen it? ______________________________
Why might they say it? ______________________________

CASE 12 · YEAR 10 · TEACHER NOTE
Teacher note
Draft, pending consultation with Aboriginal communities of the towns visited, especially 
Moree and Walgett, and those they name, and with AIATSIS guidance.
The opener
The notebook is constructed. It is not an original 1965 page, and the handwriting is not original. 
That fact belongs only in this teacher note, not on the student page. The writer is an unnamed city 
student on the bus, in the spirit of diaries kept on the trip; the page is not Ann Curthoys’s diary and 
must not be taught as hers. The date is 20 February 1965, the second Moree visit, after the first 
meeting and after the ban was put back on. Scene details — the reimposed ban, the hostile crowd, 
spit, eggs, tomatoes, stones, the police warning, Perkins taken from the gate, a child knocked down, 
frightened children, going in, and leaving in single file while things were still being thrown — follow 
Ann Curthoys’s contemporary diary (AIATSIS collection; published 2002) and Charles Perkins’s 
later account of the return, as quoted on the AIATSIS Freedom Ride page. The draft’s “four nights 
ago,” the 16 February date, the SAFA title, the method-explaining paragraph, the 88-to-10 vote, the 
by-law wording, the number aboard, Gary Williams, and Lismore were taken off this page. They 
belong in What is agreed, Super Sleuths, or this note.
Two short conversations in the source draft — a twelve-year-old who had never been inside, and a 
woman from the mission — were invented details inside a known sequence. They have been cut. 
Two scene lines were checked against the 20 February record and kept. “Charlie wouldn’t move 
from the gate. They grabbed him.” Curthoys’s diary of the return, as quoted by AIATSIS, records: 
“Charlie started talking to the crowd, but there was a lot of hissing and booing. Then he went to the 
front of the line and when he refused to move was grabbed and taken away from the line.” Perkins, 
in A Bastard Like Me (1975), also quoted by AIATSIS, places the struggle at the gate: “The mayor 
ordered the police to have us removed from the gate entrance. They took hold of my arm and the 
struggle started.” The notebook’s “from the gate” is a short compression of those two accounts of the 
same confrontation. “One of the children was knocked down.” Curthoys’s diary, as quoted by 
AIATSIS, records: “One child had been knocked down. The poor kids were very frightened.” She 
wrote that the children told the students this, and that they had also been subjected to racist abuse 
(the wording is not repeated on the student pages). Contemporary newspaper headlines of 21–22 
February 1965 report a violent confrontation at Moree (among them the Daily Mirror, 21 February, 
and the Sydney Morning Herald, 22 February). This file did not independently recover those two 
exact phrases from a Trove article body. The closing is now: “A man at the bus said it quietly.” then 
“They’ll wait till you’re gone.” Both the speaker and the line are constructed. The man is not a 
named historical person. Do not teach either as a documented 1965 quotation. The line stands in for 
a documented pattern: after the first Moree visit the ban was reimposed once the bus had left, and 
later Moree memory records a similar fear. In 2025, Gomeroi man Uncle Darryl French, who was on 
the bus to the pool on the return visit, recalled people saying that when the students left, local 
people would have to deal with it (ABC News, 22 February 2025). Living people, including French, 
are not given dates on the student pages.

pages.text:
Reopen the Record: Australian Histories · sample · 176
Corrections and flags
Two Moree visits, not one. The source draft merged them. First visit, Wednesday 16 February 
1965: a picket; children at first refused, then let in; an evening public meeting at the Memorial Hall, 
initially hostile, at which a motion to remove the segregation clause was carried 88 votes to 10 
(Curthoys’s diary, via AIATSIS; also ABC News, 2025). On 17 February, after the students had left, 
Aboriginal children tried to get in after school; the mayor then said the 6 June 1955 statute would be 
enforced (Curthoys, 18 February entry). In Tenterfield the students voted to return. Second visit, 
Saturday 19–Sunday 20 February: a hostile crowd; eggs, tomatoes, stones, spit and scuffles; the 
mayor said he would sign a motion to rescind, with conditions; children and students went in; they 
left that night in single file (Curthoys’s diary; Perkins, A Bastard Like Me, via AIATSIS; ABC News, 
2019 and 2025). Do not teach the ban as settled on 16 February. Curthoys later recalled that it took 
about six months before the council formally rescinded the rule (ABC News, 27 September 2019).
Route and Lismore. The students left Sydney around midnight on Friday 12 February. A day-by-
day itinerary published by AIATSIS is: 12 Sydney; 13 Wellington; 14 Gulargambone; 15 Walgett; 16 
Moree (first); 17 Boggabilla; 18 Tenterfield, then back; 19–20 Moree (return); 21 Grafton; 22 
Lismore and Cabbage Tree Island; 23 Bowraville; 24 Kempsey; 25 Taree; 26 Sydney. They did not 
leave for Lismore after the first Moree meeting. Some other lists add towns such as Warwick, Glen 
Innes, Inverell or Coffs Harbour; treat those as a minor conflict in the route lists, not a problem to 
resolve on the student page.
Numbers aboard. Twenty-nine students left Sydney on 12 February (University of Sydney; 
Sydney Barani; AIATSIS). About 35 took part in all, because some left and others joined (AIATSIS). 
Keep 29 as the departure figure, and flag that the complement changed.
By-law wording. The draft shortened the rule to “No person being a full-blooded or half-caste 
aboriginal… shall use the baths.” ABC News (22 February 2025) quotes a fuller wording, used in 
Super Sleuths with a content note. Wording and spelling vary slightly across later accounts; this file 
has not checked the 1955 council instrument itself. The statute is often dated 6 June 1955 
(Curthoys).
Gary Williams. A Gumbaynggirr-Bundjalung student, and one of two Aboriginal students at the 
University of Sydney with Perkins. He was a member of SAFA, but he was not on the bus from 
Sydney and he was not at either Moree visit. He was called home for a family emergency and joined 
at Bowraville on 23 February, later confining his activism to locations on his own country 
(University of Sydney, 2024; NSWALC; Sydney Barani; ABC News, 2025). The draft’s line that he 
was “meant to join us later” and would “only come on the stretch that is his own country” over-
explains the delay. He is living: no dates on the student pages. He is named only in Super Sleuths 
and this note.
Perkins’s words and graduation. “The problem is out in the open now” is kept, cited from 
AIATSIS as said at the 1965 FCAATSI conference in Canberra, to about 200 people. This file has not 
independently checked a 1965 conference transcript. The phrase “second class is not good enough” 
appears in later interviews and education pages; it has not been pinned here to a 1965 primary 
source, and it is not used on the student pages. Do not call Perkins “the first Aboriginal person to 
graduate.” He graduated from the University of Sydney in 1966, and is often described as the first 
Aboriginal man to do so; Margaret Valadian graduated from the University of Queensland in the

CASE 13 · YEAR 10 · MABO AND TERRA NULLIUS, 1982–1992 · READ
Mabo and terra nullius, 1982–1992
Was Australia ever really treated as ‘nobody’s land’?
What is agreed
Green on this page marks what can be agreed. Amber, used in Super Sleuths, marks what is still disputed or was 
added later.
Eddie Koiki Mabo was a Meriam man from Mer (Murray Island) in the Torres Strait. In May 
1982 he and other Meriam plaintiffs, including David Passi, Sam Passi, Celuia Mapo Salee and 
James Rice, began a case in the High Court about ownership of land on the Murray Islands.
While the case was running, the Queensland Parliament passed the Queensland Coast Islands 
Declaratory Act 1985. Section 3 declared that, on annexation, the islands “were vested in the 
Crown in right of Queensland freed from all other rights, interests and claims of any kind 
whatsoever.” Section 5 said no compensation “was or is payable.”
In Mabo v Queensland (No 1), decided 8 December 1988, the High Court held that the 1985 Act 
was invalid to the extent it was inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth). The 
land case could go on.
Eddie Mabo died on 21 January 1992. On 3 June 1992, in Mabo v Queensland (No 2), six of the 
seven High Court justices held that the common law of Australia can recognise native title, and 
that the Meriam people were entitled, as against the whole world, to the possession, use, 
occupation and enjoyment of most of the lands of the Murray Islands (subject to some particular 
Crown interests).

Eddie Koiki Mabo
Meriam man of Mer (Murray Island) · lead plaintiff · died 21 January 1992, 
before the High Court decided the land case
Interviewed on his land at Las, Mer, in 1989, and remembered in later 
museum and film records.
What they said
The National Museum quotes him: “My father told me: ‘Son, this land will 
belong to you when I die.’” In 1989, on the land at Las, he said: “There were 
a total of 18 generations before my grandfather’s time that occupied this 
land and of course, from my grandfather to my father and myself makes it 
up to 20 generations all together. That we’ve occupied this area.” He 
described how later, after the London Missionary Society came, people 
were moved to the front village.
Could they have seen it?
He was speaking about his own family’s land and Meriam memory, not 
about a Latin phrase in a law book. He was a plaintiff, not a judge. He did 
not live to hear the judgment of 3 June 1992.
Why might they say it?
To say, on the record, that the land at Las had been held through 
generations, and that it would belong to him when his father died. This file 
keeps his recorded words, and does not invent what he would have said on 
the day of the judgment.
Source. The line about his father is quoted by the National Museum of Australia on its Mabo 
defining-moment page. The longer account of generations at Las is from an interview filmed 
by Trevor Graham at Las in 1989 (Yarra Bank Films; transcript published via 
mabonativetitle.com). These are his recorded words, not a speech invented for this file.

Justice Brennan
Justice of the High Court of Australia · leading reasons in Mabo (No 2), 3 June 
1992
A written judgment, not a speech from the street.
What they said
Brennan J wrote that “the fiction by which the rights and interests of 
indigenous inhabitants in land were treated as non-existent was justified by 
a policy which has no place in the contemporary law of this country.” He 
also wrote: “It is imperative in today’s world that the common law should 
neither be nor be seen to be frozen in an age of racial discrimination.” He 
said the common law “would perpetuate injustice if it were to continue to 
embrace the enlarged notion of terra nullius and persist in characterizing 
the indigenous inhabitants of the Australian colonies as people too low in 
the scale of social organization to be acknowledged as possessing rights and 
interests in land.”
Could they have seen it?
He was deciding a case in 1992, from evidence and earlier law, including 
findings made in the Queensland Supreme Court. He was not an eyewitness 
to 1788, or to life on Mer. A judgment is an official interpretation of the law, 
written for a reason, by a judge in the majority.
Why might they say it?
To explain why the Court would no longer treat Indigenous people as if they 
had no rights in land, and to give reasons for recognising native title in 
Australian common law.
Source. Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1, Brennan J. The 
judgment is on AustLII.

The State of Queensland
Defendant in the Mabo litigation · Parliament of Queensland, 1985
The government’s case, in the words of a statute passed while the Meriam 
claim was already before the courts.
What they said
The long title was “An Act to allay any doubts that may exist concerning 
certain islands forming part of Queensland.” Section 3 declared that, on 
annexation, “the islands were vested in the Crown in right of Queensland 
freed from all other rights, interests and claims of any kind whatsoever and 
became waste lands of the Crown.” Section 5 declared: “No compensation 
was or is payable to any person” by reason of the annexation, or in respect 
of any right, interest or claim alleged to have existed before it, or by reason 
of any later disposal.
Could they have seen it?
This is not one person’s memory. It is a Parliament changing, or trying to 
declare, the legal consequences of annexation in 1879. The High Court in 
1988 treated the declarations as an attempt to extinguish the very rights the 
Meriam plaintiffs were claiming. A statute can be evidence of a 
government’s position. It is not evidence of how the islands were actually 
occupied.
Why might they say it?
The Act’s own title said it was to “allay any doubts.” Passed while the 
Meriam case was already before the courts, it tried to declare the islands 
free of other rights, with no compensation. Students can ask what that 
timing shows.
Source. Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act 1985 (Qld), assented to 15 April 1985, ss 3 
and 5. The High Court later held the Act invalid, to the extent of inconsistency with the Racial 
Discrimination Act, in Mabo (No 1) [1988] HCA 69.

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
1. The phrase debate
Brennan J describes a “fiction” that treated Indigenous land rights as non-existent, and an “enlarged 
notion of terra nullius.” Historians and some lawyers, including David Ritter, have asked when the 
Latin phrase itself was first used in Australian law, and whether earlier official language used other 
words for a similar idea.
Question. What changes when a later Latin label is treated as if it had been the official slogan of 
1788?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
2. The 1985 Act, and Mabo (No 1)
The Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act was assented to on 15 April 1985, while the Meriam 
case was already before the courts. In 1988 the High Court held it invalid to the extent it clashed with 
the Racial Discrimination Act 1975.
Question. Why might a government pass a declaratory Act after a land case has already begun, and 
what did the 1988 decision change?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
3. He never heard the judgment
Eddie Koiki Mabo died on 21 January 1992. The High Court decided Mabo (No 2) on 3 June 1992. 
This file does not invent what he would have said that day.
Question. What does a gap like that ask you to do, and what does it ask you not to do?

STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
4. What the 1992 orders did, and did not do
The Court recognised native title, and Meriam rights in most of the Murray Islands, subject to some 
particular Crown interests. The Native Title Act 1993 followed. This file does not pretend the decision 
“gave the land back” in a simple way to all First Nations people, and it does not try the later cases.
Question. What can one judgment settle, and what does it leave open?
STILL IN DISPUTE, OR ADDED LATER
5. Fact-finding on Mer
Fact-finding by Moynihan J in the Queensland Supreme Court did not accept all of Eddie Mabo’s 
particular claims to individual land. The High Court still recognised Meriam native title in most of 
the islands. Both of those things can be true at once.
Question. Why might a court accept a people’s title, and still not accept every individual claim made 
in the evidence?
